docs.title: FuzzTLA
docs.text:
FuzzTLA tests the TLA+ model checkers TLC and Apalache. It generates random TLA+ specifications, checks each one with both tools, and keeps every specification on which they disagree, fail or crash. A campaign therefore finds defects in either checker and documents where their semantics differ.

Under active development

Input and output formats, configuration keys and corpus layouts may change without notice. Initialize a new corpus after upgrading FuzzTLA.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  G[Generate] --> P[Parse with SANY]
  P --> T[TLC]
  P --> A[Apalache]
  T --> C[Compare verdicts]
  A --> C
  C --> Q[Select inputs for mutation]
  Q -. next generation .-> G
  1. Generate. FuzzTLA turns random bytes into a well-typed TLA+ module. The same bytes always produce the same module.
  2. Parse. SANY, the TLA+ parser, must accept the module.
  3. Check. TLC and Apalache check the module with the same Init, Next and invariant, independently and in parallel.
  4. Compare. If the verdicts differ, for example a pass against a counterexample, the entry is a disagreement.
  5. Select and mutate. Agreeing entries that exercise the checkers well seed the next generation of inputs.

Every input, verdict and diagnostic is stored in a corpus, a directory you can resume, inspect, query and report on.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
• Getting started: build FuzzTLA and run your first campaign.
  • The corpus: what a campaign stores and what the verdicts mean.
  • Running campaigns and Configuration: control what is generated and how the checkers are run.
  • Inspecting a corpus: turn a disagreement into a TLA+ module you can rerun, and classify crashes against known issues.
  • Results: the defects and conformance differences found so far.

docs.title: Campaign report
docs.text: script/report.py turns a corpus into one Markdown report of the campaign: how it ran, what it found, and how good its inputs are.

docs.title: 1. Running
docs.text:
python3 -m pip install -r script/requirements.txt   # once: cbor2, matplotlib
python3 script/report.py corpus66
python3 script/report.py corpus66 --db corpus66/.report/corpus.sqlite

fuzztla report --corpus DIR prints these commands.

  • CORPUS: the corpus directory.
  • --db FILE: use an existing export-db database instead of exporting again.
  • --no-lock: export without the corpus lock while a run uses the corpus; the export is then not a consistent snapshot (corpus-database manual §1).
  • --max-cpus N: threads of the export.
  • --fuzztla PATH: the launcher, by default bin/fuzztla of this checkout.

Without --db, the script runs fuzztla export-db --force into .report/corpus.sqlite, which takes about 2 minutes for 300,000 entries. The rest takes under a minute. The script fails if the database's schema version is not the one it reads, or if the triager rejects the corpus.

The checkers are those the entries record, so a corpus without a .checkers file, which FuzzTLA writes only for a non-default checker set, is reported correctly.

The Corpus triage workflow writes the report of its short campaign, checks that every section and embedded image exists, and uploads report.md with its images as a workflow artifact.

docs.title: 2. Output
docs.text:
Path Content report.md The report .report/*.png One image per plot; a run removes the images of the previous one .report/config.toml Copy of the run configuration, linked from the report .report/corpus.sqlite The export, unless --db names another file

The script writes nothing else into the corpus. In particular, it classifies crashes and disagreements with the triager's signatures in memory and does not write *-triage.csv.

docs.title: 3. Contents
docs.text:
Summary. Inputs admitted and aggregated, disagreements and crashed inputs per triage class, the documented defects reproduced, the NEW and STATE_COUNT entries to investigate, and candidates filtered by known-defect signatures.

1. Campaign.

  • Setup: technique, checkers, versions, and selected configuration values.
  • Time: wall-clock span and sessions. A pause of more than 15 minutes between stage records starts a new session. Run and worker time come from .workflow-stats.cbor.
  • Stages: records per verdict, duration percentiles, timeouts and worker time.
  • Generator: candidate outcomes and the origin of admitted inputs.
  • Entries per directory.

2. Findings.

  • Verdict pairs of aggregated inputs.
  • Triage labels per crash and disagreement directory, linked to their finding or conformance document. Up to 25 NEW and STATE_COUNT entries per directory are listed with their checker results.
  • Known-defect signatures: candidates matched, samples stored, references.
  • Entries the export could not decode or replay.

Entries are cited by the first 8 hexadecimal digits of their hash.

3. Input quality. The plots below, and two collapsible tables:

  • every construct, with its index and the share of inputs whose evaluated code contains it, overall and per outcome. The index orders constructs by the number of inputs that contain them, most first; the pair heatmap uses it for its axes;
  • pairwise construct coverage: every unordered pair of constructs that occur together in the evaluated code of at least one checked input, with the number and the share of such inputs, and the indices of both constructs. The text gives how many of the possible pairs of the constructs seen occur, and names the uncovered pairs when there are at most 25.

The report groups checked inputs into four outcomes: selected (04quality-pass), agreeing, not selected (03aggregator-pass and 04quality-fail), disagreeing (03aggregator-fail), and crashed (any crash directory). An input that sits in several directories is counted once. Exploration metrics come from TLC, or from TLC-n when the corpus does not run TLC.

docs.title: 4. Plots
docs.text:
Plot Section Shows Throughput 1 Stage records over wall-clock time, cumulative and per minute Generation funnel 1 Admitted, mutant, agreeing and selected inputs per generation; median distinct states of the selected inputs Checker times 1 ECDF of stage durations per verdict, with the timeout Discovery curve 1 Cumulative disagreements and crashed inputs per triage class against inputs parsed Verdict pairs 2 Heatmap of verdicts for each pair of checkers Triage labels 2 Entries per triage label and directory Known-defect signatures 2 The 20 signatures that matched the most candidates Verdicts and failure codes 2 Share of each stage's records by verdict and failure code Input size 3 Input bytes and evaluated nodes per outcome; evaluated nodes against distinct states State-space shape 3 ECDFs of state counts, depths and discovering actions, selected against other agreeing inputs Shallow patterns and state values 3 Shallow patterns of agreeing inputs, collection size, value nesting, state size, richness cohorts and scores Operator coverage 3 Rarest constructs, constructs over-represented in disagreements and crashes, and operator edges seen per generation Pairwise construct coverage 3 Heatmap over construct indices of the share of inputs that contain both constructs; uncovered pairs in red

A plot without data, for example the verdict pairs of a one-checker corpus or the signatures of a corpus without .workflow-stats.cbor, is replaced by a note.

Lift is the share of a group's inputs that contain a construct divided by the share of all checked inputs that contain it. The report shows lifts above 1 for constructs in at least 5 inputs of the group.

docs.title: 5. Limits
docs.text:
• The corpus records no tool versions. The report shows those of the checkout that runs it.
  • Stage times have whole-second resolution, so short durations show as 0 or 1 s.
  • .workflow-stats.cbor is written on controlled exits only; a killed run adds nothing to run and worker time.

docs.title: Background
docs.text: ADR 0020 records the design.

docs.title: Collection sizes
docs.text: Generated modules rarely hold non-empty collections in a state: a starved expression falls back to {}, <<>> or a function over an empty domain, and random input rarely continues a literal past one element. A base size makes collections default to a configured size. Input bytes then make each collection smaller or larger than the base.

docs.title: 1. Configuration
docs.text:
[generator]
max_collection_size = 8
# Size of a set or sequence literal, and of a collection terminal, when the input is exhausted.
collection_base_size = 3
# Input bytes move a collection's size within base ± spread.
collection_size_spread = 4
# Maximum atoms in one generated collection value, over all nesting levels.
max_value_atoms = 64
Key Meaning collection_base_size Size a collection decodes to without input. 0 keeps terminals empty. Must not exceed max_collection_size. collection_size_spread How far input bytes move a size from the base, in 0..127. max_value_atoms Bound on the scalars inside one collection literal or terminal; nested collections share it.

docs.title: 2. What changes in a module
docs.text:
With collection_base_size = 3, a starved expression of type Set(Int) becomes {1, 2, 3} instead of {}, a Seq(Str) becomes <<"1", "2", "3">>, and a function of type Int -> Bool becomes [x \in {1, 2, 3} |-> FALSE]. A set of Booleans has at most two elements, and nested collections share max_value_atoms. A set or sequence literal drawn from input has between base − spread and base + spread elements, clamped to 1..max_collection_size.

Only the elements of values follow the base. The number of Next disjuncts, CASE arms, LET definitions, conjuncts and record fields is drawn as before.

docs.title: 3. Choosing a base
docs.text:
Larger bases put larger values into states, and make SUBSET and function sets exponentially more expensive for both checkers. Start with a base of 3 to 6 and compare, per corpus, the TLC failures in Init, maxCardinality, maxStateNodes and timeouts (exploration-metrics manual, corpus-database manual).

Changing any of the three keys reinterprets stored inputs: a corpus must keep the values it was created with.

docs.title: Background
docs.text: ADR 0011 records the design and the evaluation that chose the default base size of 3.

docs.title: Community Modules
docs.text: A community-module campaign compares the TLA+ Community Modules, as TLC evaluates them (including Java overrides), with Apalache's own definitions of the same operators.

docs.title: 1. Setting up a corpus
docs.text:
make community-modules
./bin/fuzztla init --corpus corpus-cm --library libraries/community-modules.toml
./bin/fuzztla run --how=pbt --corpus corpus-cm

make community-modules downloads the latest CommunityModules.jar release into libraries/community-modules/, and writes VERSION with its release tag and commit. Rerun it to pick up a newer release.

init --library FILE reads [generator] classpath and custom_operators from FILE, whose paths are relative to FILE. It copies each classpath entry, plus a sibling VERSION, into <corpus>/tla/, and writes the corresponding keys into config.toml. Every other setting is the default. The corpus therefore keeps the release it was initialized with; the replay manifest rejects a changed JAR. To move to a newer release, initialize a new corpus.

docs.title: 2. Linkage
docs.text:
custom_operators = [
  { module = "FiniteSetsExt", operators = ["SumSet", "Max"], link = "instance" },
]
link Apalache input Parser and TLC input "inline" (default) the module's definitions the same definitions "instance" the definitions Apalache imports for EXTENDS <Module>, which are its rewired ones for the modules it rewires INSTANCE <Module> resolved on generator.classpath, with its Java overrides "diff" the definitions of <Module>, typechecked as root INSTANCE <tlc_module>, a different module with the same operators (recursive operators)

With link = "instance", the TLC source declares one named instance per module and one alias per operator, for example:

Custom46…I == INSTANCE FiniteSetsExt
Custom46…N53… (p1) == Custom46…I!SumSet(p1)

print --spec shows this source, and print --apalache-ir the JSON Apalache reads. Replaying it outside fuzztla requires <corpus>/tla/CommunityModules.jar on TLC's class path.

docs.title: 3. Selected operators
docs.text: libraries/community-modules.toml selects the first-order operators of Apalache's rewired SequencesExt, FiniteSetsExt, Functions and BagsExt that pass library validation. Operators whose results depend on CHOOSE are included; their disagreements may reflect underspecified semantics. Reverse, ReplaceAll, InsertAt, Zip, IsSuffix, IsStrictSuffix, SeqOf, TupleOf, BoundedSeq and ReplaceAllSubSeqs are excluded until apalache-json-003 is fixed.

docs.title: 4. Findings
docs.text: Cite the CommunityModules commit from <corpus>/tla/VERSION besides the fuzztla, TLC and Apalache commits.

docs.title: Background
docs.text: ADR 0014 records the design and the probe behind it.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Each corpus has a config.toml, written by fuzztla init. The file is commented, and this page lists every key by table. Paths in the file are relative to the file itself.

You may leave out a checker table ([workflow.tlc], [workflow.tlcn], [workflow.apalache]) or any of its keys, as well as [metamorphic], [graph], checkers and the max_entries key of a stage table. Anything left out takes the default shown below. The other keys are required. Some settings are recorded by the first run and cannot change afterwards: checkers, the technique (--how), and the operator library. To change those, initialize a new corpus.

docs.title: [generator]: what is generated
docs.text: Key Default Meaning kind "module" "module" generates whole modules with variables, actions and properties. "expr" generates one expression and wraps it in a fixed single-state module. "graph" generates a module over a control graph, whose verdict the graph predicts; run --how=gbt requires it (Graph-based testing). max_type_depth 3 Maximum nesting of generated types, such as a set of functions to sequences. max_expression_depth 32 Maximum depth of an expression tree. max_nodes 128 Maximum nodes of an expression tree. max_collection_size 8 Maximum elements of a set, sequence, tuple or record literal. collection_base_size, collection_size_spread 3, 4 Typical collection size and how far input moves it (Collection sizes). max_value_atoms 64 Maximum scalars in one collection value, over all nesting levels. max_string_bytes 32 Maximum length of a string literal. max_integer_bytes, integer_base, integer_literal_spread, integer_literals 16, 1, 4, "boundary" How integer literals are drawn (Integer literals). max_variables 3 Maximum state variables of a module. max_auxiliary_operators 2 Maximum state-free operator definitions a module may use. max_action_operators 2 Maximum action definitions the next-state relation may use. max_actions 3 Maximum disjuncts of Next. max_action_parameters 2 Maximum \E parameters of one action. max_action_depth 3 Maximum nesting of \/, /\ and IF within one disjunct of Next; 0 keeps each disjunct a flat conjunction. max_steps 5 Steps from an initial state. A step counter guards Next, so the state space is finite. max_fairness 2 Maximum weak and strong fairness conditions (Actions and temporal properties). ignore ["unbound", "exotic"] Categories of expressions not to generate (below). weights { name = 8, enum_set = 16 } Relative frequency of expression forms (below). classpath, custom_operators [] Operator libraries to generate calls to (Custom operators).

docs.title: Excluding categories
docs.text:
Every expression form belongs to one category. Listing a category in ignore excludes its forms and everything that depends on them. For example, ignoring set also excludes bounded quantifiers and functions, because their domains are sets. ignore = [] enables everything.

action, temporal, unbound, exotic, control, label, operator, quantifier, bool_logic, arithmetic, set, finite_set, universe, sequence, function, fold, tuple, record, variant, model.

unbound covers unbounded quantifiers and CHOOSE (\A x : P, \E x : P, CHOOSE x : P), which neither checker can evaluate in general. exotic covers operators that one or both checkers do not support: \cdot, -+->, and temporal \EE and \AA. Both are ignored by default. The core category provides literals and fallbacks and cannot be ignored.

docs.title: Weighting forms
docs.text: weights maps the lowercase name of an expression form, such as plus, fold_set or temporal_forall, to a weight. A form with weight N is chosen N times as often as a form of weight one. Unlisted forms have weight one. Custom operators are weighted as "Module!Operator".

docs.title: [workflow]: campaign size and checkers
docs.text: Key Default Meaning max_entries 1000 Unique entries after which the campaign stops, across all directories. checkers ["tlc", "apalache"] Checkers to run, a subset of tlc, tlcn and apalache. With one checker, nothing is compared. Fixed by the first run.

docs.title: [workflow.inputs]
docs.text: Key Default Meaning max_entries workflow.max_entries Maximum inputs waiting for the parser. known_defects the shipped database Known-defect signature files. Matching candidates are quarantined instead of checked. [] checks every candidate. known_defect_samples 100 Quarantined entries kept per signature. Further matches are only counted.

docs.title: [workflow.parser], [workflow.tlc], [workflow.tlcn], [workflow.apalache]
docs.text: Key Default Meaning max_entries workflow.max_entries Maximum entries in the stage's result directories. timeout_sec 30 Time limit per input. A slower run is a crash with a timeout diagnostic. max_heap_mb 512, Apalache 1024 Heap of each checker JVM. Not for the parser. workers TLC 1, TLC-n 4, Apalache half the processors For TLC and TLC-n: TLC worker threads per input. For Apalache: concurrent Apalache processes. Must not exceed --max-cpus.

docs.title: [pbt]: random inputs
docs.text:
Property-based testing generates inputs from random bytes. Random modules tend to have few and small collections, so inputs are sorted into richness cohorts. A cohort admits only modules whose collection literals are large enough, which balances simple and rich inputs.

Key Default Meaning max_input_bytes 10240 Maximum length of a random input. Lengths are drawn from logarithmic buckets 0–3, 4–7, 8–15, and so on. richness_cohorts 10 Number of cohorts. Cohort 0 admits every module. richness_nesting_base 2.0 Weight of each level of collection nesting in the richness score. richness_threshold_base 1.5 Cohort c > 0 requires a score of at least richness_threshold_base^(c-1).

If a cohort cannot be filled after 10,000 candidates, the run stops and reports the best score it saw. Lower richness_cohorts or richness_threshold_base, or ignore fewer categories.

docs.title: [mutator]: generations and mutation
docs.text: generation_size, select_fraction, feedback_ratio, max_edits, weights, shallow_patterns, cell_capacity and feature_coverage control how each generation is selected and mutated. They are described in Generations and mutation.

docs.title: [metamorphic]: rewrites
docs.text: rules, weights, max_rewrites, max_rewrite_depth, max_rewrite_growth, base_corpus and adopt_ratio are used only by run --how=mt. They are described in Metamorphic testing.

docs.title: [graph]: control graphs
docs.text:
Key Default Meaning min_graph_nodes 20 Minimum nodes of the control graph of a graph input. The graph has a spine 0 -> 1 -> ... -> N-1, so it is up to N - 1 steps deep. max_graph_nodes 32 Maximum nodes. Node 0 is initial. max_extra_successors 2 Maximum successors of one node besides its spine successor: back edges, self-loops and forward skips of at most two nodes. max_steps max_graph_nodes Cap on the step bound. Each input draws its own bound between half its node count and its node count minus one. max_guards 2 Maximum tautological guards of one edge, when rules is set. rules absent Rule module of the edge guards, as { module = "Rewrites", classpath = ["../libraries/rewrites"] }. Absent, edges have no guards. weights {} Selection slots per guard rule, overriding its @weight annotation; 0 disables a rule.

The keys apply to graph inputs only (Graph-based testing). Their data variables and expressions use the [generator] keys; [generator] max_steps does not apply to them. Setting or changing rules changes how every graph input decodes, so a corpus records the rule module in .rewrite-library and refuses a different one.

docs.title: Corpus database
docs.text:
fuzztla export-db turns a corpus into one SQLite file. After that, questions such as "which agreeing entries are shallow", "which mutation operators pay off", "failure codes by cohort" or "which operators are overrepresented in disagreements" are SQL queries instead of scripts over thousands of CBOR files.

The database is derived data. Every export builds a new file from the corpus, and no command updates it or reads it back. When the corpus changes, or when a new build changes the schema version, export again.

docs.title: 1. Exporting
docs.text:
fuzztla export-db --corpus corpus23                     # writes corpus23/corpus.sqlite
fuzztla export-db --corpus corpus23 -o /tmp/c23.sqlite  # another location
fuzztla export-db --corpus corpus23 --force             # replace an existing file
fuzztla export-db --corpus corpus23 --no-lock           # export while a run uses the corpus
fuzztla export-db --corpus corpus23 --max-cpus=4        # replay inputs on 4 threads
  • --corpus DIR: the corpus directory. The default is corpus, as for init and run.
  • -o, --output FILE: the database file. The default is corpus.sqlite in the corpus root.
  • --force: replace FILE if it exists. Without it the command refuses and leaves the file unchanged, including a file created while the export runs.
  • --no-lock: do not take the corpus lock. By default the export takes the same exclusive lock as fuzztla run, so it fails while a run holds the lock and a run cannot start during an export. With --no-lock, the export reads a corpus that a run keeps changing. An entry that moves while the export lists its directories may appear in two directories or in none, and an entry that disappears before it is read is counted as vanished and skipped.
  • --max-cpus N: the number of threads that replay inputs. The default is all available processors, as for run.

The export writes a temporary file next to FILE and renames it to FILE only after it succeeds, so a failed export leaves no partial database. On success it prints one line, for example:

exported 1344 entries (0 unreadable, 0 replay failures, 0 vanished) to corpus23/corpus.sqlite

The export reads every entry directory of the corpus layout, from 00-inputs and 00-known-defects to 04quality-fail. It does not read .stacktrace sidecars, .work/generator-crash, or .workflow-stats.cbor.

Besides the envelope, the export replays every entry's input through the generator, as fuzztla print --corpus does, and counts the operators, LET-IN forms and literals of the resulting module (section 2.6). Replay uses the corpus's config.toml and fails if the corpus's custom operator library has changed. Replay dominates the export time: about 1.2 ms of CPU per entry, so a corpus of 100,000 entries takes about two minutes on one thread. The export writes rows in the same order for every --max-cpus, so the database does not depend on it.

docs.title: 2. Schema
docs.text:
PRAGMA user_version holds the schema version, currently 9. Any change to a table, column or view increments it. Old databases are not migrated; export them again.

Table and column names are camelCase. A column that stores an envelope field has that field's name.

Types are SQLite storage classes. A column marked null holds NULL when the envelope does not record its value. Timestamps are ISO-8601 text in UTC with milliseconds (2026-09-15T12:40:03.000Z). The fixed width makes text order chronological, and SQLite's date functions accept the format.

docs.title: 2.1. export
docs.text:
One row per property of the export.

Column Type Null Meaning Source key TEXT no corpus, exportedAt, fuzztlaVersion or technique – value TEXT no The corpus's absolute path, the export start time, the fuzztla --version string, or the technique the corpus runs (pbt, mt or gbt) –

docs.title: 2.2. entry
docs.text:
One row per entry file, keyed by id. (hash, directory) is unique: one input can sit in several directories at once, for example 02tlc-pass and 02apa-pass while the other checker is still running, and each copy has its own stage records.

Column Type Null Meaning Source id INTEGER no Row id, referenced by stage, knownDefect, mutationOperator and expr – directory TEXT no Directory name, such as 03aggregator-pass file path hash TEXT no SHA-256 of the input bytes, from the file name file name kind TEXT no expr, module or graph kind inputBytes INTEGER no Size of the generator input input cohort INTEGER yes Richness cohort of the admission gen.cohort richness REAL yes Richness score of the admission gen.richness generation INTEGER yes Generation that admitted the entry (mutation) gen.generation parent TEXT yes For a mutant, the hash of the entry it was mutated from; for an adopted entry, of its parent in the base corpus gen.parent evaluatedNodes INTEGER yes Subexpressions the checkers evaluate (section 2.6); NULL when replay failed replayed input replayError TEXT yes Why replaying the input failed; NULL when it succeeded replayed input

docs.title: 2.3. knownDefect
docs.text:
One row per known-defect signature an entry matched when it was generated. The key is (entryId, position). Signatures are not matched again during export.

Column Type Null Meaning Source entryId INTEGER no entry.id – position INTEGER no Position in the list; 0 is the primary signature gen.knownDefects signature TEXT no Signature id gen.knownDefects

docs.title: 2.4. mutationOperator
docs.text:
One row per mutation operator applied to a mutant, in the order applied. The key is (entryId, position). An entry that was not mutated has no rows.

Column Type Null Meaning Source entryId INTEGER no entry.id – position INTEGER no Position in the list; 0 is the first edit gen.operators operator TEXT no Operator name, such as random_byte or splice gen.operators

docs.title: 2.5. rewriteRule
docs.text:
One row per rewrite rule a metamorphic entry applied, in the order applied. The key is (entryId, position). An entry of a pbt corpus, and one that could not be replayed, has no rows.

Column Type Null Meaning Source entryId INTEGER no entry.id – position INTEGER no Position in the list; 0 is the first rewrite replay rule TEXT no Rule name, a definition of the rule module such as PlusZero replay

docs.title: 2.6. stage
docs.text:
One row per stage record of an entry. The key is (entryId, stage). An entry in 03aggregator-pass has four rows: parser, tlc, apalache and aggregator; an entry in 04quality-pass or 04quality-fail also has a quality row. A stage that this build does not know still gets a row if its record has a verdict and both times.

Column Type Null Meaning Source entryId INTEGER no entry.id – stage TEXT no parser, tlc, apalache, aggregator or quality key in stages verdict TEXT no pass, counterexample, fail or crashed stages.<stage>.verdict startTime TEXT no When the stage started stages.<stage>.startTime endTime TEXT no When the stage finished stages.<stage>.endTime durationMillis INTEGER no endTime minus startTime; stages record whole seconds derived code INTEGER yes Checker failure code: 75, 120 or 150 (ADR 0003) stages.<stage>.code detail TEXT yes One-line failure detail, at most 80 characters stages.<stage>.detail phase TEXT yes init, explore or complete stages.<stage>.metrics.phase saturated INTEGER yes 1 if a value walk hit its node cap, 0 if not; NULL without metrics stages.<stage>.metrics.saturated initStates INTEGER yes Distinct initial states stages.<stage>.metrics.initStates distinctStates INTEGER yes Distinct reachable states stages.<stage>.metrics.distinctStates generatedStates INTEGER yes Generated states, duplicates included stages.<stage>.metrics.generatedStates projectedStates INTEGER yes Distinct states without the step variable stages.<stage>.metrics.projectedStates depth INTEGER yes Largest depth of a new state stages.<stage>.metrics.depth projectedDepth INTEGER yes Largest depth of a new projected state stages.<stage>.metrics.projectedDepth actions INTEGER yes Sub-actions of the next-state action stages.<stage>.metrics.actions actionsFired INTEGER yes Actions that produced a transition stages.<stage>.metrics.actionsFired actionsDiscovering INTEGER yes Actions that produced a new state stages.<stage>.metrics.actionsDiscovering maxStateNodes INTEGER yes Largest value node count of a state stages.<stage>.metrics.maxStateNodes maxCardinality INTEGER yes Largest collection in a state stages.<stage>.metrics.maxCardinality maxNesting INTEGER yes Deepest value nesting in a state stages.<stage>.metrics.maxNesting traceLength INTEGER yes Transitions in the counterexample stages.<stage>.metrics.traceLength

The metric columns, from initStates to traceLength, follow section 2 of the exploration-metrics manual, which defines each metric exactly. A metric the checker did not measure is NULL, not 0. Entries checked before exploration metrics existed have NULL in every metric column.

docs.title: 2.7. expr
docs.text:
One row per construct that occurs in an entry's evaluated code: an operator application, a LET-IN, or a literal. The key is (entryId, name).

The evaluated code is what the checkers evaluate. The walk starts at the definitions Init, Next, Inv, Spec, Prop and Liveness and follows every reference to another top-level definition. A top-level definition that nothing references is skipped. Inside reached code, every LET definition is walked. Labels are transparent. This is the walk that known-defect signatures match against.

name is the construct's name in the IR JSON of fuzztla print --apalache-ir:

  • Operator application ("kind": "OperEx"): its oper field, for example SET_ENUM, FUN_APP, OPER_APP for an application of a user-defined operator, or Sequences!Head for a standard module operator.
  • LET-IN ("kind": "LetInEx"): LetInEx.
  • Literal ("kind": "ValEx"): the kind of its value. That is TlaInt, TlaStr, TlaBool or TlaDecimal for a scalar, and TlaBoolSet, TlaStrSet, TlaIntSet, TlaNatSet or TlaRealSet for a predefined set such as BOOLEAN or Nat.

Operator names are upper case or qualified with !, so they never collide with the other two. Names (NameEx), such as variables and parameters, are not counted; they count towards entry.evaluatedNodes only.

Column Type Null Meaning Source entryId INTEGER no entry.id – name TEXT no Operator name, LetInEx, or literal value kind, as in Apalache's IR JSON replayed input occurrences INTEGER no Occurrences of the construct in the evaluated code replayed input

docs.title: 2.8. exprEdge
docs.text:
One row per edge between constructs of an entry's evaluated code, as the walk of section 2.6 visits it. An edge joins a construct to a construct that is its immediate argument, or to the body of a LET-IN, once labels are removed. Names are not constructs, so an edge never passes through a name: the body of a referenced definition has no parent. The key is (entryId, parentName, childName). The quality gate's coverage features are derived from these edges and from expr (what the gate keeps).

Column Type Null Meaning Source entryId INTEGER no entry.id – parentName TEXT no The enclosing construct, named as in expr.name replayed input childName TEXT no The argument construct, named as in expr.name replayed input occurrences INTEGER no Occurrences of the edge in the evaluated code replayed input

docs.title: 2.9. unreadable
docs.text:
One row per entry file that does not decode as a corpus envelope. The export continues past such files. The key is (directory, hash).

Column Type Null Meaning Source directory TEXT no Directory name file path hash TEXT no Digest from the file name file name error TEXT no The decoder's diagnostic –

docs.title: 2.10. verdictPair
docs.text:
A view with one row per entry that has an aggregator stage record. It puts the checkers' results side by side. A corpus that runs a subset of the checkers ([workflow] checkers) has null columns for the others.

Column Type Null Meaning Source entryId INTEGER no entry.id – hash TEXT no entry.hash – cohort INTEGER yes entry.cohort – aggregator TEXT no Aggregator verdict, pass or fail stage.verdict tlc TEXT yes TLC verdict; null when the corpus does not run TLC stage.verdict tlcCode INTEGER yes TLC failure code stage.code tlcTraceLength INTEGER yes TLC counterexample length stage.traceLength tlcn TEXT yes TLC-n verdict (TLC-n); null when the corpus does not run TLC-n stage.verdict tlcnCode INTEGER yes TLC-n failure code stage.code tlcnTraceLength INTEGER yes TLC-n counterexample length stage.traceLength apalache TEXT yes Apalache verdict; null when the corpus does not run Apalache stage.verdict apalacheCode INTEGER yes Apalache failure code stage.code apalacheTraceLength INTEGER yes Apalache counterexample length stage.traceLength

docs.title: 2.11. Indexes
docs.text: Besides the keys, stage(stage, verdict) is indexed. expr has no index on name: on corpus22 it would add 61 MB and save at most 0.1 s per query. The unique key (hash, directory) also serves lookups by hash. Every table except entry is stored WITHOUT ROWID.

docs.title: 3. Example queries
docs.text:
Entries per directory:

SELECT directory, count(*) FROM entry GROUP BY directory ORDER BY directory;

Verdict pairs of aggregated entries:

SELECT tlc, apalache, count(*) AS entries
FROM verdictPair GROUP BY tlc, apalache ORDER BY entries DESC;

Entries whose completed TLC and TLC-n searches found different numbers of distinct states (verdicts):

SELECT p.hash, t.distinctStates AS tlc, n.distinctStates AS tlcn
FROM verdictPair p
JOIN stage t ON t.entryId = p.entryId AND t.stage = 'tlc'
JOIN stage n ON n.entryId = p.entryId AND n.stage = 'tlcn'
WHERE t.phase = 'complete' AND n.phase = 'complete'
  AND t.distinctStates <> n.distinctStates;

The shallow patterns over agreeing entries, each entry assigned the first pattern that matches. An agreeing entry sits in 03aggregator-pass until the quality gate moves it to 04quality-pass or 04quality-fail, so agreement is selected by the aggregator's verdict rather than by directory. Entries checked before exploration metrics existed count as no metrics:

SELECT CASE
         WHEN t.phase IS NULL THEN 'no metrics'
         WHEN t.verdict = 'pass' AND t.initStates = 0 THEN 'vacuous pass'
         WHEN t.verdict = 'counterexample' AND t.phase = 'init' THEN 'initial-state violation'
         WHEN t.verdict = 'fail' AND t.phase = 'init' THEN 'early failure'
         WHEN t.actionsDiscovering = 0 THEN 'no discovering action'
         WHEN t.projectedStates <= 1 THEN 'counter-only progress'
         ELSE 'none of the above'
       END AS pattern,
       count(*) AS entries
FROM verdictPair p
JOIN stage t ON t.entryId = p.entryId AND t.stage = 'tlc'
WHERE p.aggregator = 'pass'
GROUP BY pattern ORDER BY entries DESC;

Admissions, gate passes and agreement per generation (mutation):

SELECT e.generation,
       count(*) AS entries,
       sum(e.parent IS NOT NULL) AS mutants,
       sum(p.aggregator = 'pass') AS agreeing,
       sum(e.directory = '04quality-pass') AS selected
FROM entry e LEFT JOIN verdictPair p ON p.entryId = e.id
WHERE e.directory NOT IN ('00-known-defects', '02apa-inputs', '02apa-pass',
                          '02apa-counterexample', '02apa-fail', '02apa-crash')
GROUP BY e.generation ORDER BY e.generation;

The yield of each mutation operator: how many of the mutants it took part in the gate selected. A mutant with stacked edits counts once per operator:

SELECT m.operator,
       count(DISTINCT e.id) AS mutants,
       count(DISTINCT CASE WHEN e.directory = '04quality-pass' THEN e.id END) AS selected
FROM mutationOperator m JOIN entry e ON e.id = m.entryId
GROUP BY m.operator ORDER BY selected DESC;

Apalache failure details by cohort:

SELECT e.cohort, s.code, s.detail, count(*) AS entries
FROM entry e JOIN stage s ON s.entryId = e.id
WHERE s.stage = 'apalache' AND s.verdict = 'fail'
GROUP BY e.cohort, s.code, s.detail ORDER BY entries DESC LIMIT 20;

TLC time per verdict:

SELECT verdict, count(*) AS entries,
       round(avg(durationMillis)) AS meanMillis, max(durationMillis) AS maxMillis
FROM stage WHERE stage = 'tlc' GROUP BY verdict;

Verdict pairs of the entries whose evaluated code applies Sequences!Head:

SELECT p.tlc, p.apalache, count(*) AS entries
FROM expr o JOIN verdictPair p ON p.entryId = o.entryId
WHERE o.name = 'Sequences!Head'
GROUP BY p.tlc, p.apalache ORDER BY entries DESC;

How much more often each operator occurs in entries that TLC passes and Apalache fails than in all aggregated entries:

WITH total AS (SELECT count(*) AS n FROM verdictPair),
     subset AS (SELECT count(*) AS n FROM verdictPair WHERE tlc = 'pass' AND apalache = 'fail')
SELECT o.name,
       sum(p.tlc = 'pass' AND p.apalache = 'fail') AS inSubset,
       round((sum(p.tlc = 'pass' AND p.apalache = 'fail') * 1.0 / (SELECT n FROM subset))
             / (count(*) * 1.0 / (SELECT n FROM total)), 2) AS lift
FROM expr o JOIN verdictPair p ON p.entryId = o.entryId
GROUP BY o.name HAVING inSubset >= 5 ORDER BY lift DESC LIMIT 15;

Evaluated code size per verdict pair:

SELECT p.tlc, p.apalache, count(*) AS entries,
       round(avg(e.evaluatedNodes)) AS meanNodes, max(e.evaluatedNodes) AS maxNodes
FROM verdictPair p JOIN entry e ON e.id = p.entryId
GROUP BY p.tlc, p.apalache ORDER BY entries DESC;

Join a triage report of script/triager.py after importing it with the sqlite3 shell:

.import --csv corpus22/03aggregator-fail-triage.csv triage
SELECT t.*, p.tlc, p.apalache FROM triage t JOIN verdictPair p ON p.hash = t.entry_hash;

The column names of the imported table come from the CSV header.

script/report.py runs many of these queries and plots their results; see the campaign-report manual.

docs.title: Background
docs.text: ADR 0009 records the design and its rationale.

docs.title: The corpus
docs.text: A corpus is the directory of one campaign. It holds the configuration, every input generated so far, and the verdict of every tool on it. Each stage of the pipeline reads entries from one directory and moves them to the directory of its verdict, so the place of a file tells you how far it got and what happened to it.

docs.title: Directory layout
docs.text:
fuzztla init creates this layout:

Directory Contents config.toml The campaign's configuration. 00-inputs/ Generated inputs waiting for the parser. 00-known-defects/ Candidates that match a known-defect signature, kept as samples instead of being checked. Created on the first match. 01parser-pass/, -fail/, -crash/ Parser verdicts. SANY must accept every generated module, so a fail or crash here is a generator bug or a SANY defect. 02tlc-inputs/, 02apa-inputs/, 02tlcn-inputs/ Parsed inputs waiting for TLC, Apalache and TLC-n, one copy per configured checker. 02tlc-<verdict>/, 02apa-<verdict>/, 02tlcn-<verdict>/ Checker verdicts: pass, counterexample, fail or crash. 03aggregator-pass/ Entries on which all checkers agree. 03aggregator-fail/ Disagreements. These are the main output of a conformance campaign. 04quality-pass/, 04quality-fail/ Agreeing entries that the quality gate kept or dropped as parents for mutation. .work/ Temporary files and generator crash artifacts. Not part of the corpus.

Other tools add files at the corpus root: triage CSV files, corpus.sqlite from export-db, and report.md from the campaign report.

02tlcn-* is used only when tlcn is among the checkers (Running campaigns).

docs.title: Entries
docs.text:
An entry is a CBOR file named by the SHA-256 hash of its content, for example 00-inputs/13d4df05….cbor. Equal inputs have equal names, so the corpus never holds duplicates. An entry stores:

  • the input bytes from which FuzzTLA regenerates the TLA+ module deterministically;
  • how it was made: its generation, richness cohort and score, and for a mutant its parent and mutation operators;
  • one record per stage, with the verdict, a failure code and message, timestamps, and exploration metrics.

The module itself is not stored. Use fuzztla print to see it. An entry can be replayed only with the generator settings of its corpus.

A crash also writes a .stacktrace file next to the entry, with the exception or the timeout diagnostic.

docs.title: Verdicts
docs.text:
Verdict Meaning pass The checker completed its search and found no violation. counterexample The checker found a state or behaviour that violates the invariant or property. fail The checker reported an error, such as an evaluation error, a type error or an unsupported operator. The entry records a failure code that classifies it. crash The checker process threw an unexpected exception, ran out of memory, or exceeded its timeout.

The aggregator waits until every configured checker has a verdict other than crash. It moves an entry to 03aggregator-pass when all verdicts are equal: all pass, all counterexample or all fail. Failure codes are not compared. Any other combination goes to 03aggregator-fail, including a counterexample from only one checker. Two TLC runs that both complete must also report the same number of distinct states. In a graph-based corpus, every checker must in addition report the verdict the graph predicts, or fail.

An entry that crashes a checker stays in that checker's crash directory and is not compared.

docs.title: What the checkers are asked
docs.text: The parser and TLC receive a TLA+ module, and Apalache receives typed Apalache IR JSON for the same module. Both check the generated Init, Next and invariant Inv with deadlock checking disabled, and the generated temporal property when there is one (Actions and temporal properties). A step counter bounds every behaviour, so both tools explore the same finite state space.

docs.title: Custom operators
docs.text: FuzzTLA can generate calls to operators from your own TLA+ modules, alongside the standard operators. A library campaign therefore tests both checkers on the operators that your specifications use. The Community Modules and recursive-operator campaigns are prepared libraries of this kind.

docs.title: Adding a module
docs.text:
Put the module in the corpus, for example in my-corpus/tla/MyOperators.tla:

---- MODULE MyOperators ----
Singleton(value) == {value}
Contains(values, value) == value \in values
====

Then list it in the [generator] table of config.toml:

classpath = ["./tla"]
custom_operators = [
  { module = "MyOperators", operators = ["Singleton", "Contains"] },
]
weights = { name = 8, enum_set = 16, "MyOperators!Contains" = 8 }
  • classpath lists directories and JARs, in search order, relative to config.toml. A JAR may hold Module.tla at its root or under tla2sany/StandardModules/.
  • operators names the operators that become expression forms. The helpers they use are included automatically.
  • Each operator has weight one unless weights names it as "Module!Operator".

Before generating, FuzzTLA runs Apalache's type checker on each module once to infer the operators' types. @type annotations are respected, and polymorphic operators get new type instances at each call.

docs.title: What an operator may use
docs.text:
An operator must be first-order and state-free. It cannot use:

  • operator parameters or operator results;
  • CONSTANTs, VARIABLEs or ASSUME;
  • recursion, except with link = "diff" (below);
  • actions or temporal operators.

Its types must be ones the generator can produce. Reals, old-style records, sparse tuples, and empty records, variants or tuples are not supported. Overriding a standard module is not supported.

docs.title: How the checkers see the operators
docs.text:
By default, every checker receives the operator definitions inlined into the generated module. A module entry can change this with link:

link Parser and TLC Apalache none inlined definitions inlined definitions "instance" the module, through INSTANCE, including its Java overrides inlined definitions, or its own built-in version of the module "diff", with tlc_module = "M" module M, which defines the same operators the entry's own module

"instance" tests TLC's Java overrides against Apalache. "diff" compares two implementations of the same operators. Only the Apalache side is validated, so the TLC side may be recursive.

docs.title: Starting from a library file
docs.text:
A library file is a TOML file with a [generator] table that holds classpath and custom_operators:

fuzztla init --corpus my-corpus --library libraries/community-modules.toml

init --library copies the classpath into my-corpus/tla/ and writes both keys into config.toml. The repository ships libraries/community-modules.toml and libraries/recursion.toml.

docs.title: The library is fixed per corpus
docs.text: The first run records the library's sources, the selected operators and the Apalache version in .operator-library. Later runs, and print --corpus, refuse to work with a changed library, because the old entries would no longer replay. To change the library, initialize a new corpus.

docs.title: Exploration metrics
docs.text:
Two checkers agreeing on a verdict says little when neither of them explored anything. Most agreeing pairs in current corpora are like that: TLC finds no initial state, the invariant fails in the initial state, or both checkers stop on an evaluation error before a state exists. Exploration metrics record how much a checker explored to reach its verdict. The quality gate uses them to keep only agreements that exercise the checkers.

The TLC stage measures its run and stores the result in the corpus entry. The Apalache stage stores the length of its counterexample. The checker stages do not accept or reject anything based on these metrics, and no configuration key controls them. The aggregator compares one metric: checkers whose search completed must report the same distinctStates (verdicts).

docs.title: 1. Where metrics are stored
docs.text:
Each checker stores its metrics in a metrics map under its own stage record:

{
  "kind": "module",
  "input": h'…',
  "stages": {
    "tlc": {
      "verdict": "counterexample",
      "startTime": 1(1789459200),
      "endTime": 1(1789459202),
      "metrics": {
        "phase": "explore",
        "initStates": 1,
        "distinctStates": 4,
        "generatedStates": 7,
        "projectedStates": 3,
        "depth": 3,
        "projectedDepth": 2,
        "actions": 2,
        "actionsFired": 2,
        "actionsDiscovering": 1,
        "maxStateNodes": 9,
        "maxCardinality": 3,
        "maxNesting": 2,
        "traceLength": 3
      }
    },
    "apalache": {
      "verdict": "counterexample",
      "startTime": 1(1789459202),
      "endTime": 1(1789459205),
      "metrics": { "traceLength": 3 }
    }
  }
}

Fields appear in the order of the tables in section 2, with saturated last. A count the checker did not measure is absent; for example, actions is absent when TLC stops before model checking starts. saturated appears only when it is true.

The map is written for the pass, counterexample and fail verdicts. A crashed entry has no metrics: a timeout or a dead worker JVM returns nothing to measure. On fail and counterexample, the counts cover what TLC had explored when it stopped.

The conformance aggregator copies both stage records into the merged entry unchanged, so metrics reach 03aggregator-pass and 03aggregator-fail.

docs.title: 2.1. TLC
docs.text: Field Meaning phase How far TLC got: complete if the search finished, otherwise init if it stopped before its initial states were complete and explore if it stopped afterwards. initStates Distinct initial states. distinctStates Distinct reachable states, initial states included. generatedStates Initial states plus transitions, including transitions to states already found. projectedStates Distinct states after removing step, the step counter of a generated module. In an expr entry, equal to distinctStates. depth Length of the longest shortest path from an initial state to a found state. projectedDepth The largest depth at which a new projected state appeared. actions Sub-actions TLC split Next into, including the skeleton's UNCHANGED disjunct. actionsFired Disjuncts of Next, by source location, that produced at least one transition. actionsDiscovering Disjuncts of Next, by source location, that produced at least one new state. maxStateNodes Largest state by value node count: every scalar, collection, record, tuple and function node counts one. maxCardinality Largest set, sequence, tuple, record or function domain in any state. maxNesting Deepest value nesting in any state. A scalar variable has nesting 0. saturated true if a state exceeded the node cap of the size walk. The three size fields are then lower bounds. traceLength Transitions in TLC's counterexample. A liveness trace counts its closing stuttering step or step back to an earlier state. A violation in an initial state has length 0. Present only for counterexample.

docs.title: 2.2. Apalache
docs.text: Field Meaning traceLength States in violation1.itf.json minus one. Present only for counterexample, and absent if Apalache wrote no readable trace.

docs.title: 3. Reading metrics
docs.text:
fuzztla print --envelope lists the metrics under each stage, one field per line:

stages:
  tlc:
    verdict: counterexample
    startTime: 2026-09-15T08:00:00Z
    endTime: 2026-09-15T08:00:02Z (duration: 2s)
    metrics:
      phase: explore
      initStates: 1
      distinctStates: 4
      generatedStates: 7
      projectedStates: 3
      depth: 3
      projectedDepth: 2
      actions: 2
      actionsFired: 2
      actionsDiscovering: 1
      maxStateNodes: 9
      maxCardinality: 3
      maxNesting: 2
      traceLength: 3

docs.title: 4. Recognizing shallow entries
docs.text:
These patterns show that an agreement does not exercise the model checkers. ADR 0008 estimates that 99.6% of the agreeing entries of corpus22 match at least one of them.

Pattern Metrics What happened Vacuous pass verdict pass, initStates: 0 Init is unsatisfiable. TLC checks nothing and passes. Initial-state violation verdict counterexample, phase: init Inv or Prop fails on an initial state. Next is never evaluated. Early failure verdict fail, phase: init TLC fails before its initial states are complete. Next is never evaluated. No discovering action actionsDiscovering: 0 No disjunct of Next reaches a new state. Counter-only progress projectedStates at most 1 Only step changes. Every other variable keeps its initial value.

The gate will combine metrics from both stages. Agreement on traceLength, and on the failure code of a fail/fail pair, is derived from the stored values rather than stored separately.

docs.title: 5. Limits
docs.text:
• Metrics come from one TLC run with the stage's settings. They describe the bounded state graph that max_steps allows, not the specification in general.
  • The TLC metrics add a callback per transition and a bounded value walk per new state. ADR 0008 measured no difference on corpus entries and about 15% on a module with 1.7 million transitions.
  • Apalache reports no state counts. It explores symbolic executions of fixed length, so traceLength is its only comparable metric.

docs.title: Background
docs.text: ADR 0008 records the design and the calibration measurements behind it. Entries checked before this feature have no metrics.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This page builds FuzzTLA, runs a small campaign, and shows where to look at what it found.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• JDK 25
  • Apache Maven 3.9.10 or newer
  • Python 3 for triage and reports (optional)

The build downloads everything else, including pinned releases of TLC and Apalache.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/tlaplus/model-checker-hardening.git
cd model-checker-hardening
make package
./bin/fuzztla --version

bin/fuzztla is the launcher. It works from any directory, so you can add bin to your PATH. It runs a private copy of the JAR, so rebuilding FuzzTLA does not disturb a running campaign.

docs.title: Your first campaign
docs.text:
Create a corpus, the directory that holds the campaign:

./bin/fuzztla init --corpus my-corpus

init writes my-corpus/config.toml with defaults and creates the stage directories. The default campaign stops at 1,000 entries. For a quick trial, lower max_entries in the [workflow] table and generation_size in the [mutator] table to 20 each. Then run:

./bin/fuzztla run --how=pbt --corpus my-corpus

--how=pbt selects property-based testing, which generates fresh random inputs and mutates good ones. In a terminal, run shows a live flow diagram of the stages and their counters. A new value is bold for one second, with an arrow showing its direction. When the run ends, it prints a summary:

Random seed: 42
Workflow run finished for 'my-corpus'
Corpus entries: 20
Total elapsed: 48s
Stop reason: COMPLETED

TLC
  Pass 0
  Cex 2
  Fail 18
  Crash 0

APALACHE
  Pass 2
  Cex 8
  Fail 8
  Crash 2

AGGREGATOR
  Agree 8
  Differ 10
...

Cex counts counterexamples, that is, invariant or property violations. Differ counts entries on which TLC and Apalache disagree. Most disagreements in a fresh corpus are already documented differences. For example, TLC reports Head(<<>>) as an error, while Apalache leaves its value unconstrained. Triage, below, separates these from new ones.

Press Ctrl+C to stop a run. Run the same command again to continue: counts accumulate across runs, and interrupted work is recovered at startup. To grow a finished corpus, raise max_entries and run again.

docs.title: Look at the results
docs.text:
Disagreements are in my-corpus/03aggregator-fail/, and checker crashes are in my-corpus/02tlc-crash/ and my-corpus/02apa-crash/. Each entry is a CBOR file named by the SHA-256 hash of its content. Print the TLA+ module of one:

./bin/fuzztla print --corpus my-corpus my-corpus/03aggregator-fail/13d4df05….cbor

Classify all crashes and disagreements against the known findings and conformance reports:

python3 -m pip install -r script/requirements.txt
python3 script/triager.py my-corpus

The triager writes one CSV file per directory, for example my-corpus/03aggregator-fail-triage.csv. Each row names an entry and the document that explains it, or NEW if no document does.

Write a campaign report with plots:

python3 script/report.py my-corpus

The report is my-corpus/report.md.

docs.text:
