  • Running campaigns covers seeds, CPU limits and the other techniques.
  • Inspecting a corpus shows how to rerun an entry with TLC or Apalache by hand.

docs.title: Graph-based testing
docs.text: A graph-based campaign generates modules whose control structure is a directed graph of 20 to 32 nodes. A spine 0 -> 1 -> ... -> N-1 makes it up to N - 1 steps deep, and extra edges add loops, cycles and short skips. A variable pc holds the current node. Each node assigns new values to the data variables, and each edge runs its source node's assignments and moves pc to its target. The invariant is pc /= k for one target node k. Because every edge is enabled, FuzzTLA knows from the graph whether a checker must report a counterexample, and how long it must be. A checker that disagrees has a defect, even when the other checker agrees with it. Optionally, edges carry tautological guards (section 4), which a correct checker always evaluates to TRUE.

docs.title: 1. Setting up a corpus
docs.text:
./bin/fuzztla init --corpus corpus-gbt
# edit corpus-gbt/config.toml as below
./bin/fuzztla run --how=gbt --corpus corpus-gbt

[generator]
kind = "graph"                # required by --how=gbt
max_variables = 3

[workflow]
checkers = ["tlc", "apalache"] # one checker is enough, see section 3

[workflow.inputs]
known_defects = ["../signatures/all-defects.toml"]

[workflow.apalache]
timeout_sec = 60              # deep spines unroll 10 to 31 steps

[graph]
min_graph_nodes = 20
max_graph_nodes = 32
max_extra_successors = 2
# max_steps = 32              # cap on each input's own step bound
rules = { module = "Rewrites", classpath = ["../libraries/rewrites"] }  # edge guards, section 4
max_guards = 2
  • The technique is fixed. The first run records gbt in .technique; later runs must pass --how=gbt. run refuses another kind.
  • Mutation works as under pbt. [mutator] feedback_ratio sets the share of byte mutants of 04quality-pass entries; random inputs fill the rest.
  • [graph] may be left out. Its keys then take the defaults above. The data variables and the expressions use the [generator] keys. Each input draws its own step bound, so [generator] max_steps does not apply.
  • Give Apalache some margin. Apalache unrolls one step per transition, and a spine is checked to a bound of 10 to 31 steps. In a first campaign it took 2 s at the median and 45 s at most; 1 entry in 300 exceeded the default 30 s.
  • Use the full defect database. A node action runs every time its node is visited, so TLC fails on a partial term, such as a function applied outside its domain, more often than in a pbt corpus. With all-defects.toml, TLC failed on 9% of the entries of a campaign, against 45% with the shipped known-defects.toml (Known-defect signatures).

docs.title: 2. What the checker sees
docs.text:
fuzztla print shows the graph, the target k and the expected outcome before the module; fuzztla print --spec shows the module alone:

nodes: 23
edges: 0 -> 1, 1 -> 2, 2 -> 3, ..., 21 -> 22, 22 -> 5, 22 -> 9
target: 19 (distance 19, step bound 13)
expected: pass
module:
---- MODULE FuzzInput ----
...

A small graph shows the shape of the module (simplified, three nodes, target 2, bound 2):

VARIABLES var0, var1, pc, step

Node0 == var0' = var0 + 1 /\ UNCHANGED var1
Node1 == var1' = var1 \cup {var0} /\ UNCHANGED var0
Node2 == var0' = 0 /\ var1' = {}

Init == var0 = 3 /\ var1 = {1} /\ pc = 0 /\ step = 0

Next ==
  \/ step < 2 /\ pc = 0 /\ Node0 /\ pc' = 1 /\ step' = step + 1
  \/ step < 2 /\ pc = 1 /\ Node1 /\ pc' = 2 /\ step' = step + 1
  \/ step < 2 /\ pc = 1 /\ Node1 /\ pc' = 1 /\ step' = step + 1
  \/ step < 2 /\ pc = 1 /\ Node1 /\ pc' = 0 /\ step' = step + 1
  \/ UNCHANGED <<var0, var1, pc, step>>

Inv == pc /= 2
  • Node 0 is initial; pc ranges over 0..N-1. The spine edges here are 0 → 1 and 1 → 2, and the extra edges 1 → 1 and 1 → 0.
  • Node<u> assigns some data variables with v' = e and leaves the others unchanged. The right-hand sides are generated expressions, as under pbt, and read neither pc nor step.
  • There is one disjunct of Next per edge, and each is guarded by the input's own step bound.
  • The target lies in the upper half of the spine, and the bound between half the spine and its length. When the target is farther than the bound, the expected verdict is a pass.

docs.title: 3. Verdicts
docs.text:
Let dist(k) be the length of a shortest path from node 0 to k, and B the step bound.

Target Expected verdict Expected trace length dist(k) ≤ B counterexample dist(k) for TLC and Apalache, at least dist(k) for TLC-n dist(k) > B, or unreachable pass —

An entry passes the aggregator when the checkers agree, as under pbt, and every checker reports the expected verdict or fails. The small example expects a counterexample of 2 steps; the 23-node graph above expects a pass, because its target is 19 steps away and its bound is 13.

  • A wrong verdict is a defect. A pass on a reachable target, or a counterexample on an unreachable one, fails the entry, whatever the other checker reports.
  • A wrong trace length is a defect. A counterexample shorter than dist(k), or a TLC or Apalache counterexample of another length, fails the entry. Both search for a shortest counterexample; TLC with several workers need not find one.
  • Failures are allowed. A partial expression, such as CHOOSE x \in {} : TRUE, makes TLC fail on any input; conformance and the known-defect signatures handle it.
  • One checker suffices. With checkers = ["apalache"], the expected outcome is the oracle.

docs.title: 4. Tautological guards
docs.text:
With [graph] rules, each edge conjoins up to max_guards guards after pc = u. A guard is an instance of a rule F(x, y) == A = B of a rewrite-rule module, with every parameter drawn as an expression over the data variables. The rule UnionSelf(S) == S = S \union S with S := var1 yields the guard below:

\/ step < 5 /\ pc = 1 /\ var1 = var1 \union var1 /\ Node1 /\ pc' = 0 /\ step' = step + 1
  • The expected outcome does not change. Every rule is valid, so a guard holds in every state. A checker that evaluates one to FALSE disables the edge, and then reports a pass or a longer trace than expected.
  • Some rules do not guard. A rule with an action-level operator, such as UnchangedPrime, a higher-order parameter, such as P(_) in ForallNotExists, or a helper definition is left out. [graph] weights reweighs the rest as [metamorphic] weights does.
  • The rules are part of the encoding. Guards take a section of the input of their own, so setting rules changes how every graph input decodes. The first run records the rule module in .rewrite-library, and later runs refuse another one.
  • A pbt corpus with graph entries decodes them with the same guards.
  • Guards start at node 0. The guard bytes, about a fifth of the input, are read edge by edge from node 0, at most 8 bytes per guard, so a short input guards the first edges of every path to the target. In a campaign whose inputs had 31 bytes at the median, 97% of the entries had a guard, but at most 8.

docs.title: 5. Triage
docs.text:
Most entries of 03aggregator-fail are conformance differences, as in a pbt corpus: TLC fails on a partial term where Apalache picks a value. An entry is a graph-oracle failure when the checkers report the same verdict, or the same failure status, and print shows another expected outcome. Compare the checkers' verdicts and traceLength (print --envelope) with the expected: line.

In a guarded corpus, such an entry points at a guard on a shortest path to the target: a checker evaluated it to FALSE. Evaluate the guard alone, in the state the trace reaches before the edge, to tell a checker defect from an unsound rule. A partial term in a guard, such as a function applied outside its domain, can make Apalache pick different values for its copies in A and B, as under metamorphic testing; the known-defect signatures cover those cases.

docs.title: 6. Limitations
docs.text:
• Only pc and trace lengths are predicted. A wrong value of a data variable is found only through conformance, or through a guard that reads it.
  • Forward skips shorten some paths: in a campaign, counterexamples were 11 to 30 steps long, and one in four was 20 or more.
  • --how=mt does not rewrite graph entries.
  • Graph modules have no temporal property.

docs.title: Background
docs.text: ADR 0023 records the design. ir-generators.md §12 specifies the encoding. The step bound comes from ADR 0007.

docs.title: Inspecting a corpus
docs.text: A corpus stores inputs as bytes, not as TLA+. This page shows how to see the module behind an entry, rerun it with a checker, and sort a corpus's disagreements and crashes into known and new issues.

docs.title: Printing an entry
docs.text:
fuzztla print --corpus my-corpus my-corpus/03aggregator-fail/<hash>.cbor
Option Prints none The generated TLA+ module, or the expression for an expr corpus. For a graph entry, first the graph, the target and the expected outcome (Graph-based testing). --spec The complete specification given to SANY and TLC. --apalache-ir The typed JSON given to Apalache. --envelope The stored metadata: how the entry was generated, and each stage's verdict, failure code, timestamps and metrics. --known-defects=FILE Also lists the known-defect signatures of FILE that match the entry.

Always pass --corpus. Without it, print uses the built-in generator defaults, which give a different module when the corpus was generated with other settings.

An envelope looks like this:

kind: module
gen:
  generation: 0
  cohort: 3
  richness: 123.0
stages:
  parser:
    verdict: pass
  tlc:
    verdict: fail
    code: 75 (spec_eval)
    detail: Attempted to apply Head to the empty sequence.
    metrics:
      phase: init
      distinctStates: 1
      …
  apalache:
    verdict: counterexample
    metrics:
      traceLength: 0
  aggregator:
    verdict: fail

docs.title: Rerunning an entry by hand
docs.text:
Write the specification to a file and run TLC on it:

fuzztla print --spec --corpus my-corpus my-corpus/03aggregator-fail/<hash>.cbor > FuzzInput.tla

The module is named FuzzInput. It defines Init, Next and Inv, and for a module with a temporal property, also Liveness. FuzzTLA runs both checkers without deadlock checking. For the exact arguments, see What each checker is asked.

To shrink a metamorphic counterexample to a smaller rewrite, use fuzztla shrink (Metamorphic testing).

docs.title: Triage
docs.text:
python3 -m pip install -r script/requirements.txt   # once
python3 script/triager.py my-corpus

The triager compares every crash and every disagreement in the corpus with the signatures of the published findings and conformance reports. It writes one CSV file per directory into the corpus root:

  • 01parser-crash-triage.csv
  • 02tlc-crash-triage.csv, 02tlcn-crash-triage.csv, 02apa-crash-triage.csv
  • 03aggregator-fail-triage.csv

Each row has two columns, entry_hash and issue. issue is one of:

Value Meaning a file name, such as head-of-empty-sequence.md The finding or conformance report that explains the entry. TIMEOUT The worker timed out, and no known slow defect matches (Timeout diagnostics). FIRST_ERROR TLC and TLC-n stopped at different errors, which is expected (Comparing TLC with itself). STATE_COUNT TLC and TLC-n completed with different numbers of distinct states. NEW Nothing explains the entry. Investigate it.

Signatures are conservative: an entry is attributed to a document only when the diagnostic, and for disagreements also the verdict pair and failure code, match. An ambiguous entry stays NEW.

To count the rows by issue:

cut -d, -f2 my-corpus/03aggregator-fail-triage.csv | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

docs.title: Beyond single entries
docs.text:
• Corpus database: export the corpus to SQLite and query it with SQL.
  • Campaign report: one Markdown report with plots of a campaign.
  • Exploration metrics: tell entries that exercise the checkers apart from shallow ones, which explore almost nothing.

docs.title: Integer literals
docs.text: Generated integers default to 1 rather than 0, and literals mix small values, arithmetic boundary values such as 2^31 − 1, and wide byte payloads.

docs.title: 1. Configuration
docs.text:
[generator]
max_integer_bytes = 16
# Closed integer terminal, and centre of small integer literals.
integer_base = 1
# Input bytes move a small integer literal within base ± spread.
integer_literal_spread = 4
# How integer literals decode: "wide" byte payloads, "small" values around integer_base,
# or "boundary" values such as 2^31 - 1 besides both.
integer_literals = "boundary"
Key Meaning integer_base Value of a starved integer expression, and centre of small literals. integer_literal_spread Small literals lie in integer_base ± spread, 0..127. integer_literals "wide": every literal is a payload of up to max_integer_bytes. "small": half small, half wide. "boundary": half small, a quarter boundary values, a quarter wide.

docs.title: 2. Boundary values
docs.text:
-1, 0, 1, 2, 15, 16, 255, 256, 32767, 32768, 65536, 46340, 46341, 2^30, 2^31 − 1, −2^31, 2^31, −2^31 − 1, 2^63 − 1.

The last three lie outside TLC's signed 32-bit range. The shipped signature integer-literal-outside-tlc-range quarantines them when they occur as literals (known-defect signatures); overflow computed by arithmetic is checked.

Changing any of these keys reinterprets stored inputs: a corpus must keep the values it was created with.

docs.title: Background
docs.text: ADR 0012 records the design and the measurements behind it.

docs.title: Known-defect signatures
docs.text: A known-defect signature describes a shape of generated TLA+ IR that a tool is already known to reject. Examples are a literal-zero divisor, which Apalache reports as Mod by zero, and the set STRING, which Apalache does not support. When a signature database is configured, the input stage checks every candidate against it. Matching candidates go to a quarantine directory instead of the parser, so SANY, TLC and Apalache spend no time rediscovering filed defects. A corpus created by fuzztla init consults the shipped database. Without a database, every candidate is admitted as before.

docs.title: 1. Enabling signatures
docs.text:
Two keys in the corpus's config.toml control the feature:

[workflow.inputs]
# Known-defect signature databases, relative to this config file.
known_defects = ["../signatures/known-defects.toml"]
# Quarantined entries kept per signature in 00-known-defects.
known_defect_samples = 100
  • known_defects lists database files. Relative paths resolve against the directory that contains config.toml. Several databases are concatenated in the listed order. The empty list turns the feature off.

fuzztla init lists the repository's signatures/known-defects.toml. For a corpus inside the repository the path is relative; the example above is what it writes for a corpus in the repository root. For a corpus elsewhere the path is absolute. If init cannot find the database, it writes the empty list and says so on standard error. - known_defect_samples caps how many matching candidates are stored per signature. Further matches are counted but not stored.

Both keys are required, like every other configuration key. A corpus created before the feature existed needs them added to its config.toml.

fuzztla run reads the databases once, at startup. An invalid database stops the run before the corpus is locked. Changing a database between runs affects only later admissions; stored entries are not re-checked.

docs.title: 2. Database file
docs.text:
A database is a TOML file with one [[signature]] table per signature:

[[signature]]
id = "modulo-by-literal-zero"
references = ["../conformance/modulo-by-zero-apalache-fails.md"]
description = "Apalache preprocessing reports Mod by zero for any literal-zero modulus."
match = ['(MOD _ 0)']

[[signature]]
id = "zero-power-zero"
references = ["../conformance/zero-power-zero-apalache-fails.md"]
description = "Apalache preprocessing reports 0 ^ 0 as undefined."
match = ['(POW 0 0)']
Key Meaning id Lowercase letters, digits and hyphens. Unique across all configured databases. Recorded in quarantined entries and in statistics, so keep it stable. references Non-empty list of the finding or conformance documents that record the defect, relative to the database file. description One sentence: what the tool does with inputs of this shape. match Non-empty list of patterns. The signature matches when any of them matches.

All four keys are required, and unknown keys are errors. Write patterns as TOML literal strings (single quotes), so that " and \ inside them need no escaping.

docs.title: 3.1. Vocabulary
docs.text:
Patterns use the names of Apalache's typed IR, exactly as fuzztla print --apalache-ir prints them. That output is the reference for writing a pattern. This IR node:

{"type": "Int", "kind": "OperEx", "oper": "MOD", "args": [
  {"type": "Int", "kind": "NameEx", "name": "step"},
  {"type": "Int", "kind": "ValEx", "value": {"kind": "TlaInt", "value": 0}}]}

is matched by (MOD step 0), and by the more general (MOD _ 0).

Operator names are case-sensitive. Standard-module operators carry their module prefix, as in Sequences!Seq, Sequences!Head, FiniteSets!Cardinality and Apalache!ApaFoldSet. Other operators are named by their IR name, not by their TLA+ notation. Examples: SET_ENUM for {a, b}, TUPLE for <<a, b>>, which includes the empty sequence <<>>, FUN_APP for f[x], SET_FILTER for {x \in S : p}, CHOOSE3 for bounded CHOOSE. An application of a user-defined operator is OPER_APP, with the operator's name as its first argument.

docs.title: 3.2. Syntax
docs.text:
Pattern Matches Example _ Any expression. (MOD _ 0) ?x Any expression. All occurrences of the same metavariable in one alternative must match equal expressions. (EQ ?x ?x) integer An integer literal with this value. 0, -3 "text" A string literal with this value. (EQ _ "a") TRUE, FALSE A Boolean literal. (AND FALSE ...) STRING, Int, Nat, BOOLEAN The predefined set; the IR prints TlaStrSet, TlaIntSet, TlaNatSet, TlaBoolSet. STRING identifier A name with exactly this spelling. (MOD step 0) (OPER p1 … pn) An application of OPER to exactly n arguments that match p1 … pn in order. (Sequences!Seq _) (OPER p1 … pk ...) An application of OPER to at least k arguments, the first k matching p1 … pk. (SET_ENUM 0 ...) (: p "T") An expression that matches p and whose type matches T. (: _ "Set(Str)") (.. p) An expression that matches p, or that has a subexpression matching p at any depth. (EQUIV (.. (GLOBALLY _)) _) (& p1 … pn) An expression that matches every p1 … pn. (& (CASE ...) (.. (GLOBALLY _))) (~ p) An expression that does not match p. (STUTTER (~ (OPER_APP Next)) _)

An identifier consists of letters, digits, _, ! and $, and does not start with a digit. In head position it names an operator, which must exist; anywhere else it names a variable, parameter or definition. The words _, TRUE, FALSE, STRING, Int, Nat and BOOLEAN are reserved, and .., & and ~ are reserved as heads.

(.. p) searches operator arguments and the declarations and body of a LET, skipping labels. It does not follow a name to the definition it refers to: a temporal operator inside a referenced definition is matched where that definition is walked, not through the reference. Combine & with .. to constrain an operator whose relevant argument position varies, such as a CASE arm.

docs.title: 3.3. Types
docs.text:
The type in (: p "T") uses Apalache's type syntax, the same syntax as the type fields printed by print --apalache-ir. Examples: Int, Str, Set(Seq(Int)), (Int -> Bool), <<Int, Str>>, { f: Int }, Tag(Int) | Other(Str).

Lowercase type variables such as a and b act as wildcards: - "Set(a)" matches any set type. - "(a -> a)" matches functions whose domain and range have equal element types. - A variable binds consistently within one alternative. - A row ending in a type variable, as in { f: Int, a } or Tag(Int) | a, matches records or variants that have the listed fields and any others.

Example: (FiniteSets!Cardinality (: _ "Set(Seq(a))")) matches the cardinality of any set of sequences.

docs.title: 3.4. Matching rules
docs.text:
• Evaluated code. A pattern is tried at every subexpression of the code the tools evaluate:
  • Init, Next, Inv, Spec, Prop and Liveness;
  • every top-level definition they reference, such as generated operators and linked custom-library definitions;
  • every LET definition and lambda inside that code, referenced or not.

A top-level definition that nothing references is skipped. A pattern is never anchored to the root. - Scaffolding. Every input has the same Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars /\ Fairness and Liveness == Fairness => Prop, and every module input of a metamorphic corpus has StepProperty == [][Step]_vars. A pattern that matches them, such as (GLOBALLY (STUTTER ...)), matches every input; exclude them with (~ p). KnownDefectScaffoldingTest fails on such a signature. - Alternatives. The alternatives in match are independent. Bindings do not carry from one alternative to another. - Metavariables. Two occurrences of ?x must match structurally equal expressions. Type annotations are not compared; use a type constraint for that. Inside (.. p), the first subexpression in pre-order that matches p determines the bindings; the parts of (& p1 … pn) bind from left to right. (~ p) reads the bindings made to its left but binds nothing. - Arity. An application matches only its exact argument count unless the pattern ends in .... - Labels. Labels are skipped, just as print --apalache-ir omits them. A pattern cannot target a label. - Determinism. Whether an entry matches depends only on its bytes, the corpus configuration and the database.

docs.title: 4. Writing a signature
docs.text:
1. Start from a known defect. Use a row of a triage report produced by script/triager.py, a document in findings/, or one in conformance/. Note the diagnostic the tool reports.
  2. Look at the IR. Print a representative entry and find the construct the diagnostic names:
bin/fuzztla print --corpus corpus12 --apalache-ir corpus12/03aggregator-fail/<sha256>.cbor
  1. Write the narrowest pattern that captures a shape the tool rejects wherever it occurs. Keep the operands the defect depends on, and use _ only for the rest. For example, write (MOD _ 0), not (MOD _ _).
  2. Check it on entries that show the diagnostic, which must match, and on entries that do not, which should not:
bin/fuzztla print --corpus corpus12 --known-defects signatures/known-defects.toml <entry>

The report lists each matching signature, its references, and the subexpression it matched, rendered as TLA+. 5. Document it. Point references at the finding or conformance document, and write a one-sentence description.

Measure a signature before relying on it. It quarantines every input whose evaluated code contains its shape. But whether a tool actually reaches the shape can depend on the tool's evaluation order, so some quarantined inputs would have passed. On a corpus sample, check two things: - most entries it matches carry the referenced diagnostic; - it catches most entries that carry that diagnostic.

A shape that rarely fails is not a signature. An example is Head of a sequence that is empty only at run time. When the referenced defect is fixed, remove or narrow the signature.

docs.title: 5. What happens on a match
docs.text:
Each check runs after a candidate has passed the richness threshold and the request-frame limit. A matching candidate is not admitted to 00-inputs:

  • Primary signature. The first matching signature, in database order, is the candidate's primary signature.
  • Storage. While fewer than known_defect_samples entries of that primary signature are stored, the candidate is written to 00-known-defects/<sha256>.cbor. Otherwise it is only counted.
  • Recorded signatures. A quarantined entry records every matching signature, primary first:
{
    "kind": "module",
    "input": h'0123af',
    "gen": {
      "cohort": 3,
      "richness": 4.0,
      "knownDefects": ["modulo-by-literal-zero", "string-set"]
    }
}
  • No stage processing. No stage processes 00-known-defects, and its entries do not count towards max_entries. Generating a quarantined input again counts as a duplicate.
  • Inspection. Inspect a quarantined entry like any other: fuzztla print --corpus DIR --spec 00-known-defects/<sha256>.cbor.
  • Cleanup. You may delete the directory between runs. The per-signature caps then start again from zero.
  • Counts. The run table reports the total number of known-defect rejections. .workflow-stats.cbor accumulates the counts across runs, keyed by primary signature:
"generator": {
  "attempts": 1500,
  "knownDefects": {"modulo-by-literal-zero": 120, "string-set": 45},
  ...
}

docs.title: 6. Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• The run stops with a database error. The message names the file, the signature id, and the column within the pattern. Typical causes:
  • an unknown operator name (check the spelling against print --apalache-ir);
  • a type string Apalache cannot parse;
  • an id used twice across databases;
  • an empty match list;
  • an unknown key.
  • A signature never matches. Common causes:
  • the argument count differs, which a trailing ... fixes;
  • the pattern follows TLA+ notation rather than the printed IR, for example a lambda appears as a LET definition;
  • the pattern wraps a label, and labels are skipped.

Use print --known-defects on an entry that should match. - "could not generate corpus entry … within 10000 attempts". A signature is too broad and rejects nearly every candidate. The message reports how many of the target's attempts were known-defect rejections.

docs.title: 7. Shipped database
docs.text:
signatures/known-defects.toml holds signatures for the Apalache limitations that dominated corpus12's checking time. They were measured on the 98,676 corpus12 entries that have an Apalache result: - Recall is the share of entries failing with the referenced diagnostic that the signature matches. - Precision is the share of its matches that Apalache failed on.

Together, the signatures match 41.5% of the entries, which took 67.9% of corpus12's Apalache time.

Id Match Defect Recall Precision modulo-by-literal-zero (MOD _ 0) Apalache reaches modulo by zero 91.2% 79.5% division-by-literal-zero (DIV _ 0) Apalache reaches division by zero 90.8% 79.4% sequence-set (Sequences!Seq _) Apalache does not support Seq(S) 100% 82.5% string-set STRING Apalache does not support STRING 100% 82.0% zero-power-zero (POW 0 0) Apalache reaches 0 ^ 0 79.9% 78.9% integer-literal-outside-tlc-range 2147483648, -2147483649, 9223372036854775807 TLC rejects integers outside 32 bits not measured not measured

integer-literal-outside-tlc-range matches the out-of-range values of the boundary literal table (integer literals). It was added without a precision measurement: a quarantined entry is not checked, and TLC rejects such a literal whenever it evaluates it. It matched 27 of 1,165 candidates in the ADR 0012 boundary corpus.

The database also holds signatures for temporal formulas that TLC cannot check (TLC temporal formula limits). Here T stands for any temporal operator: GLOBALLY, EVENTUALLY, LEADS_TO, WEAK_FAIRNESS, STRONG_FAIRNESS, and the exotic GUARANTEES, TEMPORAL_EXISTS and TEMPORAL_FORALL; each such signature lists one alternative per operator. They were measured on a 1600-module smoke corpus generated with every category but exotic enabled. Recall is the share of TLC crashes with the diagnostic that the temporal signatures together match; precision is the share of a signature's matches on which TLC crashed with it.

Id Match TLC diagnostic Recall Precision tlc-temporal-equivalence (& (EQUIV ...) (.. (T ...))) cannot handle 13 of 13, together 6 of 6 tlc-temporal-case (& (CASE ...) (.. (T ...))), and CASE_OTHER cannot handle 1 of 1 tlc-temporal-unbounded-quantifier (& (FORALL2 ...) (.. (T ...))), and EXISTS2 cannot handle 7 of 7 tlc-eventually-action (EVENTUALLY (NO_STUTTER ...)) must be of forms 16 of 16, together 16 of 17 tlc-always-action-under-temporal [][A]_v under EVENTUALLY, LEADS_TO or GLOBALLY must be of forms 2 of 2 tlc-always-action-under-connective [][A]_v under NOT, IMPLIES or OR must be of forms 3 of 3 in corpus20, together 3 of 4 tlc-fairness-under-eventuality WEAK_FAIRNESS or STRONG_FAIRNESS under EVENTUALLY or LEADS_TO must be of forms 3 of 3 in corpus20, together 3 of 4

tlc-eventually-action also matches []<><<A>>_v, which TLC checks; its seventeenth match failed an evaluation before TLC reached the property. tlc-always-action-under-connective also matches <>[][A]_v under a connective, which TLC checks. The last two signatures were measured on corpus20, where the earlier ones already quarantined their shapes, and on the smoke corpus; their fourth matches failed an evaluation before TLC reached the property.

docs.title: 7.1. Recall-first database
docs.text:
signatures/all-defects.toml is for building a corpus fast. It quarantines every candidate whose code matches a defect recorded in findings/ or conformance/, so that checking time goes only to candidates that can show new behavior.

It is a superset of known-defects.toml. Its first 13 signatures are the shipped ones, in the same order, with the same ids, descriptions and patterns, so primary signatures do not change. Use it instead of known-defects.toml; listing both defines every shipped id twice, which is an error:

[workflow.inputs]
known_defects = ["../signatures/all-defects.toml"]

The added signatures follow one rule: - Uncommon operators. When a defect depends on run-time values and the operator is uncommon in generated code, the signature matches every use of the operator. Examples are Int, Nat, SUBSET, .., ^, \div, ENABLED, WF and SF. - Frequent operators. When the operator is frequent, the signature matches only the literal shapes that fail whenever they are evaluated. Examples are f[x], CHOOSE, CASE, Head, Tail, SubSeq and %. - Function sets. [S -> T] stays admitted except in its failing special cases. A function set here is [S -> T] itself, or one IF branch, \union, \intersect or \ operand of it. The special cases are: - function-set-equality: a function set compared with = or #; - function-set-expansion: a function set that is folded, mapped, filtered, counted, unioned by UNION, or the set of an applied CHOOSE.

The remaining signatures match fixed shapes: - the TLC findings about temporal formulas; - the SANY % level-error crash; - the Apalache temporal and assignment findings; - the open PrettyWriter findings. - the Community Modules operators whose defects depend on argument values: IsInjective, AntiFunction, IndexFirstSubSeq, LongestCommonPrefix, ExistsSurjection, SumBag and ProductBag. A generated module applies a library operator through an alias named Custom<hex(module)>N<hex(operator)>, so a pattern names that alias as the first argument of OPER_APP, as in (OPER_APP Custom42616773457874N53756d426167 _) for SumBag. - variant-filter: every VariantFilter, whose Apalache encoding fails on run-time payload values (apalache-bmc-022). - set-map-duplicate-product: a set map with at least two bound variables in a fold combinator, or in the first or second bound set of another such map. Apalache counts a mapped set by its tuples rather than its distinct values, so these shapes can exceed its product guard of 1,000,000 (set-map-product-guard). - recursion-insertion-sort: every application of the recursion library's SeqInsertionSort or SetToSortedSeq, whose Apalache definitions nest ApaFoldSeqLeft and can exhaust the heap from about nine elements (apalache-performance-002). - apalache-always-action-bound: every [][A]_v other than Spec's [][Next]_vars and a metamorphic relation's [][Step]_vars. The workflow checks Prop under Fairness => Prop, where Apalache needs one more step than the lasso to report a violation of [][A]_v (apalache-temporal-005). - fold-concatenation: every application of the recursion library's SeqReverse or SeqFlatten, and every ApaFoldSet or ApaFoldSeqLeft whose combinator contains \o. Apalache can exhaust a 1 GB heap on such a fold over a few hundred elements (apalache-performance-003). On the 787 corpus53 entries with an Apalache result, it matches all 58 heap exhaustions, 178 of the 223 timeouts, and 228 of the 443 entries that Apalache completed.

The database header and AllDefectsTest list the documents that no pattern can express: - A constant FALSE invariant or property: a pattern cannot be anchored to a definition. - Labels in EXCEPT (sany-002): labels are skipped. - The order sensitivity of a fold combinator, and TLC heap exhaustion in an applied CHOOSE: these depend on operand values. - Fixed findings.

The test fails when a new finding or conformance document is neither referenced by a signature nor listed as uncovered.

Measurements, taken on 2026-09-18. Apalache 0.62.3 later fixed the defects behind function-set-empty-component, apalache-fold-singleton-membership, printer-fold-in-left-operand and printer-set-map-connective-body, and those signatures were removed, so the database now matches fewer entries than measured here: - corpus29 sample. The database matched 73.3% of a sample of 600 corpus29 entries. corpus29 was generated with known-defects.toml, so every entry in the sample had already passed the shipped signatures. The top matches by share: - choose-literal-without-witness, 57%: the generator often writes CHOOSE x \in S : FALSE; - printer-fold-in-left-operand, 48%; - enabled, 37%; - power, 33%; - division, 32%. - Function sets. Of the 34 sampled entries that contain [S -> T], 10 match a function-set signature. Every one of the 34 also matches another signature, so the total stays at 73.3%. - Fresh corpus with all categories enabled. 313 of 373 candidates above the richness threshold were quarantined, and generation completed. - Remaining disagreements. The admitted entries still produced 29 aggregator disagreements: - 16 constant FALSE invariants or properties; - 13 function applications, CASEs and CHOOSEs that failed on run-time values.

docs.title: 7.2. Metamorphic database
docs.text:
signatures/metamorphic-defects.toml is for a metamorphic corpus that checks with Apalache. List it next to all-defects.toml:

known_defects = ["../signatures/all-defects.toml", "../signatures/metamorphic-defects.toml"]

A relation module holds two copies of the base, so a construct that Apalache evaluates non-deterministically can take different values in the two copies. Its one signature, metamorphic-choose, matches every bounded and unbounded CHOOSE (choose-multiple-witnesses). In a conformance corpus it would quarantine valid inputs, so all-defects.toml does not contain it. MetamorphicDefectsTest checks that both databases load together.

docs.title: Background
docs.text: ADR 0006 records the design and its rationale.

docs.title: Metamorphic testing
docs.text:
Temporal properties are not supported yet (section 6).

A metamorphic campaign checks one model checker against itself. Each input pairs a generated module M1 with a rewrite M2 that is equivalent in TLA+, for example x rewritten as x + y - y. The checker explores one of the two and checks that its initial states and transitions satisfy the other. A violation means one of two things: - the checker evaluates the two sides differently; - a rewrite rule is unsound.

Unlike a recursion campaign, no second checker is needed. The relation can be checked by TLC alone, including on recursive definitions that Apalache rejects.

docs.title: 1. Setting up a corpus
docs.text:
Adopting elite entries of an existing conformance corpus gives the richest inputs:

./bin/fuzztla run --how=pbt --corpus corpus-conf          # conformance generations
./bin/fuzztla init --corpus corpus-mt
# edit corpus-mt/config.toml as below
./bin/fuzztla run --how=mt --corpus corpus-mt

[generator]
kind = "module"               # or "expr"

[workflow]
checkers = ["tlc"]            # default ["tlc", "apalache"]

[workflow.inputs]
# With Apalache among the checkers, also list metamorphic-defects.toml (section 3).
known_defects = ["../signatures/all-defects.toml"]

[metamorphic]
rules = { module = "Rewrites", classpath = ["rewrites"] }
weights = { AddSub = 3 }      # overrides the rule's @weight, else 1; 0 disables a rule
base_corpus = "../corpus-conf"
adopt_ratio = 0.5
max_rewrites = 16
max_rewrite_depth = 4
max_rewrite_growth = 2
  • The technique is fixed. The first run records mt in .technique. Later runs must pass --how=mt, and print and export-db read the file. A corpus without it is a pbt corpus.
  • Adopted parents. A generation takes adopt_ratio of its entries from adopted parents: the 04quality-pass entries of base_corpus, each combined with random rewrite bytes. [mutator] feedback_ratio still sets the share of byte mutants, and PBT fills the rest.
  • The base corpus is read-only. It must be a pbt corpus. It is never written to, and an entry keeps its parent's bytes, so base_corpus is not needed to replay it.
  • The base corpus decodes alike. An adopted payload decodes under the metamorphic corpus's settings, and decodes to the parent's module only if they agree. run therefore refuses a base corpus whose [generator] settings differ, or whose .operator-library differs from the library this run prepares. classpath and custom_operators are compared through .operator-library, which pins the library sources rather than their paths. Copy the base corpus's [generator] table and its library sources.
  • Adopted entries record their parent. gen.parent is the parent's digest in the base corpus, and gen.operators is ["adopt"].
  • The checker set is fixed. The first run records checkers in .checkers, and later runs must use the same list.
  • Rule weights. A rule's weight is the number of selection slots it takes among the rules that match a node. The rule module sets a default in the comment before a rule, \* @weight: 8;, and weights overrides it. The shipped Rewrites.tla weighs padding such as x + 0 1, reordering 2, value rebuilding 4, and rules that replace an operator 8.
  • The rules are fixed. The first run records the rule module's sources and the effective weights in .rewrite-library. Editing a rule or its weight requires a new corpus.

docs.title: 2. What the checker sees
docs.text:
fuzztla print --spec shows the relation module. An orientation bit in the entry chooses the explored side E and the checked side C:

Orientation E (explored) C (checked) even M1 M2 odd M2 M1

Each side's parts are definitions of their own, named by the side X ∈ {E, C}:

Definition Meaning InitX initial predicate ActionX next-state action without its stuttering disjunct InvX state invariant PropX temporal property FairnessX fairness conditions exprX the expression of an expr entry

The relation module combines them:

Entry point expr module Init v = exprE InitE Next UNCHANGED v ActionE \/ UNCHANGED vars Inv v = exprC (step = 0 => InitC) /\ (InvE <=> InvC) Step none [ActionC]_vars, an action invariant Prop none (PropE => PropC) /\ (PropC => PropE) when the base has a property
  • One copy of the variables. M2 shares M1's variables. Only its operators are renamed.
  • The action invariant. TLC checks it as PROPERTY StepProperty, where StepProperty == [][Step]_vars, and reports "Action property StepProperty is violated". Apalache checks it with --inv=Inv,Step.
  • Deadlock detection stays off, as in a conformance corpus.
  • Only the relation is checked. Whether the base invariant or property holds does not matter.
  • The explored module is unchanged. The relation reaches exactly the states of E, so the exploration metrics and the quality gate rank E.

docs.title: 3. Verdicts
docs.text:
The aggregator applies the metamorphic oracle:

Verdicts Directory every checker pass, or every checker fail 03aggregator-pass any counterexample, or checkers disagree 03aggregator-fail

A fail is not a metamorphic violation. A checker's evaluation error on a partial term, such as CHOOSE without a witness, fails both sides alike. The quality gate, known-defect signatures and the mutator work as in a conformance corpus.

Apalache evaluates CHOOSE non-deterministically, so the two copies of one CHOOSE with several witnesses may differ, and Apalache reports a counterexample without any rewrite (conformance note). A corpus that checks with Apalache should list signatures/metamorphic-defects.toml next to all-defects.toml; it quarantines every CHOOSE. A TLC-only corpus does not need it.

docs.title: 4. Triage
docs.text:
A counterexample has two possible causes:

  • An unsound rule. The rule is not an equivalence in TLA+, or it breaks the rule contract (section 5).
  • A checker defect in evaluating one side.

To tell them apart:

  1. List the rules and the orientation. fuzztla print replays them. A violation of Inv at step = 0 is an initial state of E that InitC rejects. A violation of Step is a transition of E that ActionC rejects.
  2. Reduce the stack of rewrites. fuzztla shrink --corpus corpus-mt ENTRY.cbor first checks the base related to itself, with no rule applied. If a configured checker reports a counterexample to that, it evaluates two copies of one module differently, so no rule is at fault; shrink says so and writes nothing. Otherwise it clears the rewrite markers one at a time and keeps each change after which a configured checker still reports a counterexample. It writes the reduced input to ENTRY-shrunk.cbor, which fuzztla print --corpus corpus-mt shows. The rules left are the culprits. An entry needs at least one rule, so shrink always leaves one; the check of the base is what rules out every rule.
  3. Evaluate both sides of that rule on the counterexample's last state or transition under TLC and, where possible, Apalache.
  4. If a checker disagrees with the expected value, reduce the input to an MWE and file a finding.
  5. If the rule is at fault, fix the rule. Rule changes reinterpret stored entries, so initialize a new corpus.

Findings cite the FuzzTLA commit, which versions the rules, besides the TLC and Apalache commits.

docs.title: 5. Writing rules
docs.text:
A rule is an operator of the rule module. Its body relates a pattern A to its replacement B. The shipped libraries/rewrites/Rewrites.tla has several rules per type, and a section of beta and iota redexes, such as x = LET F(v) == v IN F(x) and x = [field0 |-> x].field0. This module shows the format:

------------------------------ MODULE Rewrites ------------------------------
EXTENDS Integers, FiniteSets

PlusZero(x) == x = x + 0
AddSub(x, y) == x = x + (y - y)
DoubleNeg(P) == P = ~~P
UnionSelf(S) == S = S \union S
UnchangedPrime(x) == (UNCHANGED x) = (x' = x)
ForallNotExists(S, P(_)) == (\A e \in S : P(e)) = ~(\E e \in S : ~P(e))
AlwaysTwice(F) == []F <=> [][]F
=============================================================================
  • Every top-level definition is a rule. Put helpers in a module that the rule module EXTENDS. B may apply them, A may not. The relation module does not link helpers yet, so the shipped rules define what they need in a LET inside B.
  • Rewriting goes from A to B only. Add a second rule for the other direction.
  • A rule module can also guard graph edges. [graph] rules conjoins whole instances A = B of its rules to the edges of graph inputs, all parameters drawn (Graph-based testing). Only rules without an action-level operator, a higher-order parameter or a helper serve as guards.
  • Use <=> for temporal formulas. SANY rejects = between them.
  • Annotate when Snowcat asks. Snowcat cannot tell a tuple from a sequence, or a record from a function, by their use alone. Add \* @type: (<<a, b>>) => Bool; above such a rule.
  • Records and variants use the generator's names. A pattern names a field or a tag literally, so the shipped record and variant rules use field0 and Tag0, the first names that the generator draws.
  • Apply higher-order parameters in B. B may apply P to any term, and the rewriter beta-reduces the application. To pass P to an operator, write LAMBDA x : P(x); the loader rejects a bare P.
  • Bind names, not tuples, in B. Apalache's PrettyWriter prints a tuple binder of \A, \E or CHOOSE as one identifier, which SANY rejects. Bind a pair t and use t[1] and t[2].
  • Parenthesize. A pattern matches what SANY parses. x + y - y is x + (y - y), because binary - binds tighter than +, and UNCHANGED x = e is a precedence error.

Each parameter is one of three kinds:

Kind Where it occurs At rewrite time Example matched in A bound to a subterm of the node x in PlusZero fresh only in B drawn by the generator at its type, in the node's scope y in AddSub higher-order in A, applied to variables that A binds bound to LAMBDA e : body P(_) in ForallNotExists

Snowcat infers each rule's signature, and a rule applies only at a node of a matching type. UnionSelf applies to sets of any element type.

The loader rejects a rule that: - applies a prime, UNCHANGED, ENABLED or another action-level operator in B when A applies none, or any temporal operator; - names anything other than its parameters, bound variables, built-in operators and helpers.

The matcher skips a rule where it would move a primed equation out of an assignment position, or reorder primed conjuncts. For example, DoubleNeg does not apply to x' = 1: under ~~, TLC no longer treats the equation as an assignment. It also skips operators, such as a lambda passed to a fold, and a match that would move a label under a binder of B or into an EXCEPT replacement, where SANY rejects it.

Validity is the author's job. Prove each new rule in libraries/rewrites/RewritesProofs.tla, under the hypotheses that its signature gives (the module header lists them), and run make proofs:

THEOREM AddSubValid == ASSUME NEW x \in Int, NEW y \in Int PROVE AddSub(x, y)
  BY DEF AddSub

mvn verify fails when a rule has no such theorem, and CI runs make proofs. Before you write the proof, a quick TLC check over small domains can catch a wrong rule early: ASSUME \A x, y \in -3..3 : AddSub(x, y) in a module that EXTENDS the rule module.

docs.title: 6. Limitations
docs.text:
• One direction per entry. An entry checks only that E's initial states and transitions satisfy C. A rewrite that only adds initial states or successors is detected only by entries that explore M2. In ADR 0016's probe, one direction detected 108 of 301 perturbations, and both directions together detected 111.
  • Temporal properties are not rewritten yet. The first implementation leaves a module's property and fairness out of the relation and loads no temporal rule. Once they are added, TLC will reject some temporal relations: formulas that negate [][A]_v fail with "Temporal formulas containing actions must be of forms <>[]A or []<>A".
  • TLC-only corpora. A corpus with checkers = ["tlc"] compares no checkers, so its entries are not conformance tests.

docs.text: ADR 0016 records the design and the probes behind it, and ADR 0017 the rule format. The rule catalog will be specified in a later ADR.

docs.title: Generations and mutation
docs.text: Random generation rarely produces a module whose state changes in interesting ways. A run therefore proceeds in generations. After each generation, a quality gate keeps the agreeing entries that show a behaviour or cover code that the kept entries lack. The next generation is partly mutated from those entries and partly generated by PBT.

docs.title: 1. How a run proceeds
docs.text:
1. Admit. The input stage admits up to generation_size entries. A feedback_ratio share of them are mutants of entries in 04quality-pass, and the rest are generated by PBT. Before any entry has passed the gate, PBT generates the whole generation.
  2. Look ahead. Once the generation is admitted, the PBT share of the next generation is admitted too, while this generation's checkers are still running. Its mutant share cannot follow yet — it depends on a selection that has not happened — so only one generation is ever open ahead of the one being gated. Work and CPU from the older generation are served first.
  3. Settle. The parser, TLC, Apalache and the aggregator process every entry of the generation. An entry the parser rejects, and one a checker crashes on, settles where it is.
  4. Select. The quality gate moves each entry of the generation from 03aggregator-pass to 04quality-pass or 04quality-fail.
  5. Repeat for the next generation, until every generation that fits in workflow.max_entries has run.

The run length is counted in generations, not in stored entries: a run ends after ceil(workflow.max_entries / generation_size) generations. A generation that ends up short — because the run was interrupted, or because the corpus was written with a different generation_size — leaves the corpus below workflow.max_entries, and the run still reports that it completed.

Every entry records the generation that admitted it in gen.generation. A mutant also records gen.parent, the hash of the entry it was mutated from, and gen.operators, the edits applied:

$ fuzztla print --corpus corpus --envelope corpus/04quality-pass/<hash>.cbor
kind: module
gen:
  generation: 3
  cohort: 4
  richness: 2.0
  parent: <hash of the parent>
  operators: random_byte
…

An interrupted or stopped run resumes at the oldest generation that still lacks entries, still has work in flight, or has not been gated — at most one before the highest generation the corpus records, since only one generation is ever admitted ahead. It admits what that generation is missing, keeping the configured share of mutants, drains the pending work, and reruns the gate, which completes an interrupted selection exactly. The startup scan reconstructs this from the corpus itself; no inventory is taken between generations afterwards.

Each generation numbers its targets from 0, mutants first and PBT after, and a target's ordinal seeds the stream it draws from. A resumed generation reserves the ordinals its stored entries already used, so the entries it adds draw fresh streams. A corpus does not store target ordinals, so after an interruption the reservation is reconstructed from the counts, not from the original assignment: the entries already admitted are unaffected, but the exact streams of an interrupted run's remaining targets cannot always be replayed.

workflow.max_entries may be raised between runs to continue a corpus.

A run requires gen.generation on every entry, so a corpus written before generations existed cannot continue. fuzztla print and fuzztla export-db still read it once 04quality-pass and 04quality-fail exist.

docs.title: 2. Configuration
docs.text:
fuzztla init writes the [mutator] table with these defaults:

[mutator]
generation_size = 1000
select_fraction = 0.05
feedback_ratio = 0.5
max_edits = 1
weights = { random_byte = 8, bitflip = 8, parity_flip = 8, copy = 4, duplicate = 1, insert = 1, erase = 1, splice = 1 }
shallow_patterns = ["vacuous_pass", "initial_state_violation", "early_failure", "no_discovering_action", "counter_only_progress"]
cell_capacity = 4
feature_coverage = true
Key Meaning generation_size Entries each generation admits, and the unit the run length is counted in. With generation_size ≥ workflow.max_entries, a run is one generation. select_fraction Upper bound on the share of a generation's agreeing entries kept in 04quality-pass, rounded up. Must be in (0, 1]. feedback_ratio Share of a generation that is mutated. 0 disables mutation; the gate still runs. max_edits Cap on stacked edits per mutant. A mutant gets 1 edit, plus one more with probability ½ each, up to the cap. weights Relative weight of each operator. An omitted operator has weight 0. shallow_patterns Patterns of the exploration-metrics manual that exclude an entry from 04quality-pass. cell_capacity Entries of 04quality-pass per behaviour cell (section 3). 0 removes the bound. feature_coverage Also keep an entry that adds an operator-edge coverage feature (section 3).

With cell_capacity = 0 and feature_coverage = false, the gate keeps the best select_fraction of every generation.

The defaults come from one experiment on one corpus. Calibrate select_fraction and feedback_ratio against your corpus with the queries in section 4.

docs.title: 3. What the gate keeps
docs.text:
An entry of 03aggregator-pass is admissible when all of these hold:

  • its TLC verdict is pass or counterexample;
  • TLC recorded exploration metrics;
  • it matches none of shallow_patterns.

The gate ranks admissible entries by TLC's exploration metrics, compared in this order, higher first:

  1. projectedDepth;
  2. projectedStates, by power of two;
  3. actionsDiscovering;
  4. maxStateNodes, by power of two;
  5. maxCardinality, by power of two;
  6. maxNesting.

Ties go to the shorter input.

The gate walks the admissible entries in this order and keeps an entry while it has kept fewer than ceil(select_fraction × agreeing entries of the generation) and either of these holds:

  • Behaviour. The entry's cell holds fewer than cell_capacity kept entries. The cell is the TLC verdict together with the six metrics above, each compared as in the ranking (states, nodes and cardinality by power of two).
  • Coverage. feature_coverage is enabled and the entry has a feature that no kept entry has.

"Kept" counts 04quality-pass over every earlier generation plus the entries this generation has kept so far. Every other entry of the generation, admissible or not, moves to 04quality-fail. The mutator's parent pool is all of 04quality-pass, over every generation.

The features of an entry come from the code the checkers evaluate, the same code that the expr table of the corpus database counts. Constructs are operator applications, LET-IN, and literal kinds. The features are:

  • a construct and how often it occurs;
  • an edge, meaning a construct and a construct that is its immediate argument (SET_IN → FUN_APP, for example), and how often it occurs.

Counts are bucketed as in AFL: 1, 2, 3, 4–7, 8–15, 16–31, 32–127, 128 or more. The gate computes features by replaying the input through the generator, as fuzztla export-db does. An input that fails to replay has no features.

An expr corpus is always shallow: its module has no transitions. To exercise mutation on one, set shallow_patterns = [].

docs.title: 4. Mutation operators
docs.text:
Operator Edit random_byte Replaces one byte with a random byte. bitflip Flips one bit. parity_flip Flips the low bit of one byte. On a continuation marker it adds or removes an element of a structural list; on the size byte of a set or sequence literal it changes the size by one (collection sizes). copy Copies up to 32 bytes over another offset. duplicate Repeats a block of up to 32 bytes in place. insert Inserts up to 8 random bytes. erase Deletes up to 16 bytes. splice Joins a prefix of the parent with a suffix of another parent.

A mutant is truncated to pbt.max_input_bytes. It passes the same admission as a PBT candidate: the worker request-frame limit, duplicate detection and the known-defect signatures. The richness cohorts do not apply. A mutant whose TLA+ module is identical to its parent's is a clone and is discarded; the run table counts these as mutant clones. If a target entry cannot be filled within 10,000 candidates, the run stops with a diagnostic that names the parent pool size and the rejection counts.

After fuzztla export-db (corpus-database manual), the yield of each generation and operator is a query:

SELECT e.generation, count(*) AS entries, sum(e.parent IS NOT NULL) AS mutants,
       sum(e.directory = '04quality-pass') AS selected
FROM entry e
WHERE e.directory NOT LIKE '02apa-%' AND e.directory <> '00-known-defects'
GROUP BY e.generation ORDER BY e.generation;

SELECT e.generation, count(DISTINCT x.parentName || ' ' || x.childName) AS edges
FROM entry e JOIN exprEdge x ON x.entryId = e.id
WHERE e.directory = '04quality-pass'
GROUP BY e.generation ORDER BY e.generation;

SELECT m.operator, count(DISTINCT e.id) AS mutants,
       count(DISTINCT CASE WHEN e.directory = '04quality-pass' THEN e.id END) AS selected
FROM mutationOperator m JOIN entry e ON e.id = m.entryId
GROUP BY m.operator ORDER BY selected DESC;

docs.title: 5. Determinism
docs.text: A run replays given the same seed, configuration and starting corpus, for any --max-cpus: every target entry draws from a stream seeded by the run seed, its generation and its position in the generation. The one exception is two targets that draw identical bytes, where scheduling decides which one stores them. A resumed generation is not a replay of the uninterrupted one.

docs.title: Background
docs.text: ADR 0010 records the design and the experiment behind it. ADR 0013 revises the quality gate: behaviour cells and operator-edge coverage.

docs.title: Recursive operators
docs.text:
A recursion campaign compares TLC's evaluation of recursive definitions with Apalache's evaluation of equivalent non-recursive definitions. Every library operator comes as a pair of modules:

  • the TLC module uses RECURSIVE, LET RECURSIVE, mutual recursion or recursive functions;
  • the Apalache module uses folds or closed forms.

The aggregator compares their verdicts.

docs.title: 1. Setting up a corpus
docs.text:
./bin/fuzztla init --corpus corpus-rec --library libraries/recursion.toml
./bin/fuzztla run --how=pbt --corpus corpus-rec

The library ships with fuzztla, so nothing is downloaded. init copies libraries/recursion/ into <corpus>/tla/recursion/, and the corpus keeps that copy.

docs.title: 2. Linkage
docs.text:
[generator]
classpath = ["recursion"]
custom_operators = [
  { module = "RecursionApalache", link = "diff", tlc_module = "RecursionTLC",
    operators = ["SetSum", "SetSumLetRec", "SeqReverse"] },
]
link Apalache input Parser and TLC input "diff" the definitions of module, typechecked as root INSTANCE <tlc_module>, resolved on generator.classpath

module provides the signatures and the mangled names; richness scoring and known-defect matching use its definitions. fuzztla never imports tlc_module: only SANY and TLC read it. The TLC source declares, for example:

Custom52…I == INSTANCE RecursionTLC
Custom52…N53…(CustomP1) == Custom52…I!SetSum(CustomP1)

Library preparation parses these declarations once and stops if tlc_module, an operator, or a matching arity is missing. print --spec shows the TLC source, and print --apalache-ir the JSON Apalache reads. To replay a TLC input outside fuzztla, put <corpus>/tla/recursion/ on TLC's class path.

docs.title: 3. Writing a pair
docs.text:
A disagreement must mean a defect. Each pair therefore follows these rules:

  1. Same interface. Both modules define each selected operator with the same arity.
  2. The Apalache module passes library validation: first-order, supported syntax, no recursion.
  3. The TLC module is constant-level.
  4. Apalache 0.62.2 generalizes the type of a parameter that only LET definitions constrain: F(n) == LET k == n + 1 IN k gets (a) => Int (apalache-typechecker-001). The generator then passes any value to F, and Apalache computes arbitrary values or crashes in its rewriter. Give such operators an explicit @type. RecursionLibraryIntegrationTest pins which exports are polymorphic.
  5. Equal and total. Both sides agree on every argument of the Apalache signature. Define edge cases explicitly on both sides: empty sets and sequences, and negative integers. Never evaluate Head(<<>>) or a CHOOSE without a witness.
  6. Order-insensitive. A recursion that picks set elements with CHOOSE combines them commutatively and associatively. Otherwise the pair reproduces order-sensitive set folds.
  7. Bounded cost.
  8. Recurse on generated collections, whose size is bounded (collection size).
  9. Clamp integer arguments of integer-driven recursion to a small constant on both sides.
  10. On the Apalache side, avoid a..b with nonconstant bounds (conformance).
  11. One name per mechanism. Export each TLC variant under its own name, and in the Apalache module define it as an alias of the shared definition:
\* RecursionTLC
RECURSIVE SetSum(_)
SetSum(S) == IF S = {} THEN 0 ELSE LET x == CHOOSE x \in S : TRUE IN x + SetSum(S \ {x})
SetSumLetRec(S) ==
  LET RECURSIVE Sum(_)
      Sum(T) == IF T = {} THEN 0 ELSE LET x == CHOOSE x \in T : TRUE IN x + Sum(T \ {x})
  IN Sum(S)

\* RecursionApalache
SetSum(S) == LET Plus(a, b) == a + b IN ApaFoldSet(Plus, 0, S)
SetSumLetRec(S) == SetSum(S)

Before a campaign, add each new operator to the pairwise self-test, src/test/resources/recursion/RecursionPairs.tla. This module instantiates both modules and asserts A!Op(x) = T!Op(x) in ASSUME over small domains, and make test runs it under TLC.

docs.title: 4. Operators
docs.text:
libraries/recursion.toml selects 39 operators from libraries/recursion/RecursionTLC.tla and RecursionApalache.tla. A suffix names TLC's recursion mechanism: none for a top-level RECURSIVE operator, LetRec for LET RECURSIVE, Fun for a recursive function definition, and HO for a higher-order RECURSIVE helper. Operators without a suffix may use more than one mechanism, as the table shows.

Group Operators TLC Apalache Sets SetSum, SetSumLetRec, SetSumFun, SetSumHO the four mechanisms, over CHOOSE ApaFoldSet SetCount, SetUnionAll, SetPowerset, SetMaxWith(S, d), SetAllPositive, SetMapDouble, SetFilterPositive RECURSIVE over CHOOSE Cardinality, UNION, SUBSET, fold, \A, map, filter SetToSortedSeq RECURSIVE on the unique minimum fold of an insertion SetTriangles LET RECURSIVE inside a set map closed form inside a set map Sequences SeqSum, SeqSumLetRec, SeqSumFun Head/Tail, tail-recursive accumulator, function on 0..Len(s) ApaFoldSeqLeft SeqReverse, SeqToSet, SeqFlatten, SeqMapDouble, SeqMapDoubleHO, SeqFilterPositive, SeqCountOf(s, x), SeqIsSorted, SeqInsertionSort RECURSIVE; HO via MapSeq(F(_), s) ApaFoldSeqLeft SeqEvenLength mutual recursion Len(s) % 2 = 0 Functions FunSumValues, FunIncrementAll LET RECURSIVE over DOMAIN, the latter through EXCEPT with @ fold, function constructor FunTriangles LET RECURSIVE inside a function constructor closed form Relations TransitiveClosure, Reachable(R, x) fixed point, frontier search Warshall fold over the nodes Integers IntTriangle (≤ 30), IntPow2 (≤ 20), IntFactorial (≤ 12), IntFib (≤ 20), IntFibFun (≤ 20) LET RECURSIVE, RECURSIVE, recursive functions, double recursion closed forms, folds over constant ranges IntDigitSum, IntGcd(a, b), IntIsEven recursion on \div 10, Euclid, mutual recursion on n % 64 fold over 0..9, six folds of 8 Euclid steps, n % 2 = 0

The bound in parentheses is the clamp. The first argument is clamped to 0..bound, with the same clamp on both sides. The Apalache folds over integer ranges apply one step independently of the element, so their value does not depend on the order in which the elements are visited.

docs.title: 5. Triage
docs.text:
A disagreement on a diff-linked call has one of three causes:

  • the pair is not equivalent;
  • TLC evaluates the recursion wrongly;
  • Apalache evaluates the fold or closed form wrongly.

To tell them apart, add the counterexample's arguments to the pairwise self-test.

  • TLC finds the two definitions equal. The operator pair agrees under TLC, so look at Apalache's evaluation of the fold or closed form, or at the context of the call.
  • TLC finds them unequal. Either the pair is not equivalent or TLC evaluates the recursion wrongly. Derive the expected value from the definitions to decide:
  • If the library is at fault, fix the pair and initialize a new corpus.
  • Otherwise, reduce the TLC side to an MWE.

Findings cite the fuzztla commit, which versions the library, besides the TLC and Apalache commits.

Two 10-minute campaigns (about 320 aggregated entries each) found no disagreement caused by a library pair:

  • Disagreements. Every disagreement matched an existing conformance or findings class, for example CHOOSE without a witness, ENABLED, or fairness.
  • Apalache timeouts. About 9% of the entries that reached Apalache timed out at the default 30 s. The timeouts track the number of library calls per input, not a single operator. Consider a larger timeout_sec for the Apalache stage of a recursion corpus.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
FuzzTLA campaigns have found defects in TLC and Apalache, and differences between them that are intended or depend on undefined expressions. Both are documented in the repository:

  • Filed findings: confirmed defects in TLC, Apalache and SANY, grouped by subsystem, each with a reproduction.
  • Conformance reports: differences between TLC and Apalache that a corpus confirmed. Each report gives the share of disagreements it explains, a classification, and a minimal TLA+ module.

The triager attributes the entries of your corpus to these documents. Entries it reports as NEW may be new findings.

docs.title: Running campaigns
docs.text:
fuzztla run --how=TECHNIQUE [--corpus=DIR] [--seed=SEED] [--max-cpus=N]
Option Meaning --how=pbt Property-based testing: generate random modules, compare the checkers, and mutate good inputs (Generations and mutation). --how=mt Metamorphic testing: check one checker against equivalent rewrites of its input (Metamorphic testing). --how=gbt Graph-based testing: check each checker against the verdict that a generated control graph predicts (Graph-based testing). --corpus=DIR The corpus directory. Default: corpus. --seed=SEED A nonnegative seed. A random seed is used when it is omitted. The seed is printed first in either case. --max-cpus=N Maximum number of jobs that run at the same time. Default: all processors.

A run admits inputs until the corpus holds workflow.max_entries entries, then finishes the work in flight and prints a summary. See Getting started for an example.

docs.title: Choosing a campaign
docs.text: Goal Setup Compare TLC and Apalache on the standard operators init, then run --how=pbt. This is the default. Compare them on the TLA+ Community Modules Community Modules Compare TLC's recursion with Apalache's folds Recursive operators Generate calls to your own operators Custom operators Test one checker against itself Metamorphic testing Check verdicts against a predicted outcome Graph-based testing Compare TLC with one worker against TLC with several Comparing TLC with itself

docs.title: Stopping and resuming
docs.text:
Press Ctrl+C to stop. The run stops its workers and saves the corpus. The next run on the same corpus validates it, finishes moves that were interrupted, and continues where the last run stopped. The counters in the summary add up over all runs of a corpus.

Only one process uses a corpus at a time. run and export-db take a lock on it.

docs.title: CPU use
docs.text: --max-cpus limits the jobs that run at the same time across all stages. A TLC job uses workflow.tlc.workers CPUs, so with --max-cpus=8 and workers = 2, at most four TLC processes run. Apalache runs workflow.apalache.workers long-lived processes, one CPU each. Checking has priority over parsing, and parsing has priority over generation, so a slow checker does not pile up unchecked inputs.

docs.title: The live display
docs.text: On an interactive terminal, run redraws a flow diagram of the stages once per second. It shows the queue and verdict counters of each stage. A changed value is bold for one second and marked ↑ or ↓. After the workers stop, FINALIZING means that the corpus is being validated. Set NO_COLOR to turn off colors. When output is redirected to a file, only the final summary is printed.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text:
Every entry can be replayed exactly. Its input bytes and the corpus's generator settings determine the module, and fuzztla print regenerates it (Inspecting a corpus).

A whole run is reproducible only approximately. Each generator worker has its own random stream derived from --seed, so the same seed, configuration, starting corpus and --max-cpus produce the same candidate inputs. Which candidates become entries, however, depends on timing between workers.

docs.title: Comparing TLC with itself
docs.text:
With checkers = ["tlc", "tlcn"] in [workflow], every input is checked by TLC with one worker and by TLC with workflow.tlcn.workers workers. The two must report the same verdict, and when both searches complete, the same number of distinct states. TLC-n can be added to a TLC and Apalache campaign as a third checker.

The triager reports a disagreement in which one TLC run finds a counterexample and the other an evaluation error as FIRST_ERROR. Multi-threaded TLC may reach either error first, so this is not a defect.

The triager reports two completed searches with different numbers of distinct states as STATE_COUNT. Rerun such an entry many times with several workers: in corpus68, one was tlc-020, a race that corrupts values shared by TLC's workers.

Older corpora

A corpus created before TLC-n existed lacks its directories. Create them with mkdir corpus/02tlcn-{inputs,pass,counterexample,fail,crash}.

docs.title: When a run stops with an error
docs.text: Message What to do could not generate corpus entry … for richness cohort … The generator cannot make inputs rich enough for that cohort. Lower richness_threshold_base or richness_cohorts in [pbt], or ignore fewer categories. parser worker did not connect within … The machine is overloaded, often by another run. Lower --max-cpus. A generator crash with a path under .work/generator-crash/ A FuzzTLA bug. The .cbor and .stacktrace files there reproduce it, so please report them.

docs.title: Actions, temporal properties and fairness
docs.text: A module corpus can generate primed guards in Next, a temporal property checked by both model checkers, and fairness conditions in the specification. Generation follows the TLA+ level rules of Specifying Systems, so SANY accepts every such module. Shapes that TLC cannot check are generated too, and the shipped known-defect signatures quarantine them (section 5).

docs.title: 1. Enabling the operators
docs.text:
fuzztla init enables the operators: it writes a module corpus whose ignore list leaves action and temporal out.

[generator]
kind = "module"
# Maximum weak and strong fairness conditions in a generated specification.
max_fairness = 2
ignore = ["unbound", "exotic"]

A corpus created before this default keeps the kind and ignore its config.toml records; edit both to enable the operators there. Add action or temporal to the ignore list to turn them off.

Category Enables action Post-assignment guards that read primed variables, the operand of ENABLED, and the actions inside [A]_v, <<A>>_v, WF and SF. temporal The property section and ENABLED: [], <>, ~>, [][A]_v, <><<A>>_v, WF and SF. ENABLED may also occur in Init, Inv, definitions and guards. exotic -+->, \EE, \AA and \cdot. Keep it ignored: specifications rarely use these forms, and TLC and Apalache both crash on them. No signature quarantines them.

Enabling action without temporal adds post-assignment guards but no property. max_fairness = 0 generates properties without fairness conditions in Spec; WF and SF can still occur inside the property formula. A corpus that ignores temporal keeps the byte layout it had before these operators existed.

In an expr corpus, which declares no state variables, these categories enable only ENABLED of constant actions. Every other action or temporal form has nothing to apply to.

docs.title: 2. What a generated module contains
docs.text:
Next == \/ step < 5 /\ guards /\ assignments /\ step' = step + 1 /\ postGuards
        \/ ...
        \/ UNCHANGED <<var0, var1, step>>
Inv == ...
Fairness == WF_<<var0>>(var0' > var0)                          \* TRUE if none
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<var0, var1, step>> /\ Fairness
Prop == [][var1' # var1]_var1 /\ \A q \in {1, 2} : (<>(var0 = q) ~> [](var1 = 0))
Liveness == Fairness => Prop
  • Post-assignment guards follow step' = step + 1. Every primed variable they mention has already been assigned.
  • The step guard and the stuttering disjunct replace the former Bound state constraint. No state beyond step = max_steps is reachable and every state may stutter, so both checkers see the same finite graph and the same infinite behaviors.
  • The property is optional. It is one temporal formula, nested as TLA+ allows: through the Boolean connectives including <=>, IF branches, CASE arms, LET bodies, quantifier bodies, [], <> and ~>. An action appears only inside [][A]_v, <><<A>>_v, WF or SF.

fuzztla print renders the whole module, including Spec, Prop and Liveness. The printer parenthesizes []([Next]_(vars)); SANY, TLC and Apalache treat it as [][Next]_vars.

docs.title: 3. What each checker is asked
docs.text:
Without a property With a property TLC configuration SPECIFICATION Spec, INVARIANT Inv adds PROPERTY Prop Apalache arguments --init=Init --next=Next --inv=Inv --length=max_steps adds --temporal=Liveness, with --length=max_steps + 1

TLC applies fairness through Spec. Apalache does not support fairness, so it is asked to check Liveness, which states the same obligation as an implication.

docs.title: 4. Expected results
docs.text:
Module contains TLC Apalache Aggregation No ENABLED, WF or SF pass or counterexample the same verdict compared as usual ENABLED anywhere evaluates it fail, "unsupported expression: ENABLED" fails; the triager classifies it as a known limitation WF or SF evaluates it fail (spec_eval), "Handling fairness is not supported yet!" fails; the triager classifies it as a known limitation A property that is constant FALSE or a tautology fail, "The property of Prop is equal to FALSE" or "Temporal formula is a tautology" checks it fails; the triager classifies it as a TLC restriction

A property that makes the parser stage fail with a level error is a decoder defect, not a SANY finding. Report it against the generator.

docs.title: 5. Shapes TLC cannot check
docs.text:
TLC cannot check some well-formed temporal formulas: a temporal formula under <=>, in a CASE arm or under an unbounded quantifier, <><<A>>_v, [][A]_v under another temporal operator or under ~, => or \/, and fairness under <> or ~>. The shipped known-defect database quarantines modules with these shapes, so they land in 00-known-defects with the signature id instead of crashing TLC. Keep known_defects pointing at signatures/known-defects.toml; without it, expect roughly 2% of generated modules to crash TLC. The conformance document lists each shape with a reproduction.

Checking a property adds one transition to Apalache's unrolling and doubles its state variables. Expect Apalache time per module to rise when temporal is enabled. In a 400-module smoke run, ENABLED and fairness accounted for 15 of 240 aggregator deviations, and a constant property for 10; ADR 0007 lists the full counts.

docs.title: Timeout diagnostics
docs.text: A parser or checker worker that exceeds its stage's timeout_sec is stopped, and the input gets a crash verdict. This page describes what the crash's .stacktrace sidecar contains, how the triager classifies it, and how to add a signature for a slow defect.

docs.title: 1. Reading a timeout sidecar
docs.text:
TLC worker timed out after PT30S
TLC worker stderr:
Tool threads at shutdown:
"TLCWorkerThread-000" RUNNABLE
    at java.lang.StringConcatHelper.prepend(StringConcatHelper.java:765)
    ...
    at tlc2.value.impl.FcnLambdaValue.toString(FcnLambdaValue.java:780)
    at tlc2.value.impl.Value.toStringImpl(Value.java:400)
    at tlc2.value.impl.Value.toString(Value.java:375)
    at tlc2.value.impl.FcnLambdaValue.apply(FcnLambdaValue.java:189)
    ...
    [537 more frames]
TLC2 Version 2026.10.21.070023
...
Progress(1) at 2026-10-21 09:00:27: 1 states generated (1 s/min), ...

This is corpus67's 5319b006, replayed: TLC was formatting the message of a function-domain error (tlc-performance-002). The sidecar has three parts:

  1. The timeout line, with the stage's limit.
  2. The tool's threads when the worker was stopped: every thread that was running or waiting for a lock, by name, innermost frame first, at most 256 frames per thread and 64 KiB in all. Waiting threads, such as TLC's main thread during exploration, and the JVM's own threads are omitted. Frames read as in an exception trace.
  3. The tool's output for the input, up to the point where it was stopped.

The stacks are one sample at the deadline. They show where the tool was, not where it spent its time. A sidecar has no stacks if the worker could not run its shutdown hook within 2 seconds, or if it ran out of heap first. A worker that ends its JVM itself, as TLC does in tlc-019, prints the same two parts after the line <Tool> worker exited while processing the input.

docs.title: 2. Triage
docs.text:
script/triager.py matches a timeout sidecar against the signatures declared for timeouts only. The first match, in catalog order, labels the entry with its finding. A timeout that no signature matches is labeled TIMEOUT. Signatures for completed tool runs are never applied to timeouts, and timeout signatures never to other crashes.

Frames in a TLC thread Label Value.toString called from FcnLambdaValue.apply, no CallStackTool frame tlc-performance-002 The same pair and a CallStackTool frame tlc-018

The campaign report (manual) uses the same signatures, so its triage table lists the timeout classes.

docs.title: 3. Writing a timeout signature
docs.text:
1. Reproduce the slow phase with the corpus's settings, for example by rendering the entry and running TLC standalone:
bin/fuzztla print --corpus corpus67 --spec corpus67/02tlc-crash/<sha256>.cbor > FuzzInput.tla
  1. Sample the stacks a few times during the slow phase, with jstack <pid> or from timeout sidecars of the same cause. Pick a sequence of frames that every sample contains and that names the cause, such as Value.toString called from FcnLambdaValue.apply for tlc-performance-002. Frames that appear in every slow input, such as Tool.getNextStates, do not name a cause.
  2. Add the signature to SIGNATURES in script/triager.py with timeout_finding, which names the finding and the patterns over the frames. The tlc-performance-002 signature reads:
TLC_FORMATTING_DOMAIN_ERROR = (
    r"^\tat tlc2\.value\.impl\.Value\.toString\([^)\n]*\)\n"
    r"\tat tlc2\.value\.impl\.FcnLambdaValue\.apply\("
)
TLC_CALL_STACK_FRAME = r"^\tat tlc2\.tool\.impl\.CallStackTool\."

timeout_finding("tlc-performance-002.md", Tool.TLC,
                all_of(TLC_FORMATTING_DOMAIN_ERROR,
                       rf"\A(?![\s\S]*{TLC_CALL_STACK_FRAME})")),

Match class and method names, not line numbers, which change with the tool's version. 4. Add a test to script/test_triager.py with a sidecar of the finding and one of an unrelated timeout, and record the instances in the finding's corpus evidence.
